item.content:encoded:
今年的诺贝尔科学奖是现实版科幻

科学与技术 | 跳出框框的思考 2026年10月8日

当威斯康星大学麦迪逊分校的弗朗西斯·哈尔岑在今年晚些时候接受他的诺贝尔物理学奖时，他将享受到难得的独自站在聚光灯下的特权。大多数物理学奖得主必须与一位合作者或竞争对手分享舞台。哈尔岑博士将是自1992年以来第一位独享所有荣誉的人。周二公布的获奖评语表彰了他“对冰立方中微子观测站的决定性贡献”，该探测器位于南极附近，占据一立方公里的冰层，汇集了14个国家450名研究者的努力。但据乌普萨拉大学物理学家、诺贝尔物理学奖委员会秘书乌尔夫·丹尼尔森所说，“没有他的科学远见，这是不可能实现的。”

探测中微子需要极大的科学远见。中微子呈电中性（因此得名“neutr-”），且体积微小（因此得名“-ino”），实际上它们既不受电磁力影响，也不受引力影响，这使得它们能穿过大多数粒子探测器而不被察觉。它们与普通物质的相互作用主要局限于通过名副其实的弱核力进行的交互。尽管中微子如同幽灵一般，但它们在宇宙中无处不在。它们是裂变和聚变反应的副产品，这使得太阳成为一个强大的近邻来源：每秒钟约有650亿个太阳中微子穿过指甲盖大小的区域。产生中微子的太阳反应也会释放其他粒子，包括质子。然而，有时到达地球的质子的能量比来自太阳的质子高出数百万倍。这表明它们来自更遥远、更强大的源头。这些天然粒子加速器究竟是什么，以及它们如何产生如此高能的粒子，在很大程度上仍是未知数。质子带电荷，因此在到达地球的途中会被磁场偏转，使其起源点难以追溯。然而，加速这些质子的相同过程也应该产生高能中微子。

在上世纪80年代，哈尔岑博士是意识到中微子不愿与物质相互作用、因此能长距离无阻碍穿行并充当来自其他不可见物体的理想信使的人之一。但探测它们仍然是个问题。此前的探测器依赖建造巨大的全氯乙烯（一种干洗液）容器，等待中微子与液体中原子之间的罕见相互作用。虽然类似的方法也可以应用于寻找更罕见的太阳系外中微子，但需要比以往建造的探测器大得多的设备才有可能捕捉到一个。于是，冰立方的想法应运而生。建设始于2004年，于2011年完成。两年之内，它捕捉到了28个高能宇宙中微子，为宇宙打开了一扇新窗口。周二，当被问及这扇窗口可能揭示什么时，通过电话联系到的哈尔岑博士回答说：“真正的兴奋之处在于我还无法回答这个问题。”

生理学或医学奖得主在概述其研究的潜在益处时可能被允许更加乐观。斯坦福大学的卡尔·德塞罗思、柏林洪堡大学的彼得·黑格曼和维尔茨堡大学的格奥尔格·纳格尔因奠定了光遗传学的基础而获得认可。这一技术使神经科学家能够利用光瞬时激活单个脑细胞，从而有可能精确确定特定细胞在做什么。这使研究人员能够研究基础神经生物学以及疾病的神经基础。

故事始于上世纪90年代的黑格曼博士。当时他正在研究一种名为衣藻的单细胞藻类属如何对光做出反应。他发现它们的反应比人眼的同等反应更快。在人眼视网膜中，一个蛋白质分子检测到光，然后间接触发另一个称为离子通道的蛋白质产生电信号。黑格曼博士假设，在他的藻类中，这一复杂的进程被压缩了。用当时可用的工具来验证他的猜测被证明是困难的，直到蓬勃发展的基因组学科学拯救了他。一组日本研究人员绘制了衣藻的DNA图谱，表明它包含两个基因，类似于某些其他生物体中光敏感蛋白的基因。当黑格曼博士获得纳格尔博士的协助时，这一见解得到了证实。纳格尔博士将新发现的两个基因的DNA插入一些青蛙的卵中，这些卵随后产生了足够数量的目标蛋白质以供测试。正如黑格曼博士所预测的那样，它们被证明是光刺激的离子通道。

意识到他们的发现后，纳格尔博士和黑格曼博士尝试将其中一个基因（编码现在称为channelrhodopsin-2的蛋白质）插入从仓鼠和人类胚胎中提取的肾细胞中。这也成功了。换句话说，他们发现了一种使哺乳动物细胞对光敏感的方法。然而，正是德塞罗思博士构想出将channelrhodopsin-2插入以其存在意义就是传递电信号的细胞——神经元中。当这个想法得到测试时，培养的大鼠神经元不仅在被光照射时做出反应，还能将信号传递给邻近的神经元。

宣布这一发现的论文发表于2005年，但其他研究人员也在探索类似的想法。三年前，当时在纽约纪念斯隆·凯特琳癌症中心工作的格罗·米森伯克使用来自果蝇的光敏感蛋白做了类似的工作。正如一些人所指出的，米森伯克博士可能有充分的理由感到恼怒。麻省理工学院的神经科学家爱德华·博伊登——他在斯坦福读博士时曾与德塞罗思博士合作——也是另一个令人惊讶的遗漏。不过，无论优先权的细节如何，这一领域此后已经爆炸式发展。德塞罗思博士的实验室引领了潮流，首先是在活体小鼠大脑中重复了在培养的大鼠细胞中所做的事情，然后发明了使用极细光学纤维照亮并从而刺激神经元群的技术。这些技巧结合起来，使研究人员能够控制小鼠胡须的运动。

光遗传学现在已经成为数千篇论文的主题。它被用于动物研究中，以探究抑郁症、精神分裂症、失明、耳聋、痴呆、成瘾和焦虑。甚至有人尝试用它来恢复一种名为视网膜色素变性的失明患者的视力。大橡树从小橡子长成。或者，在这种情况下，从小藻类长成。

化学奖，通常如此，也从生命研究中获得灵感。许多对生物学至关重要的分子是手性的，能够以两种镜像形式存在，至少在理论上，这两种形式在宇宙中应等量存在。然而，自然是无情地选择性的。对于生物体而言，氨基酸通常是左旋的；糖是右旋的。正是为了在理解这种不对称性可能如何产生方面取得进展，巴黎萨克雷大学的亨利·卡根和东京理科大学的Soai Kenso接到了来自斯德哥尔摩的电话。

在此之前，化学家已经能够选择性地生产具有给定手性的分子。但所有这些反应都依赖于手性催化剂，这种催化剂通常由不等量的左旋和右旋分子混合而成。假设是反应产物中左右旋分子的比例将与催化剂本身的比例匹配。这带来了一个问题：如果反应只能匹配催化剂的不对称性，那么大规模的不对称性又如何能出现呢？1986年，卡根博士通过发现手性催化剂可以超越这一基准，驳斥了这一假设。从催化剂中左旋分子比右旋分子多三倍开始，他可以设计出产生六倍失衡溶液的反应。这是一个有意义的改进，但仍然太小，无法将无生命物质的近乎完全对称性转变为生命所展现的近乎完全手性。

正是Soai博士弥合了这一差距。在2003年发表的工作中，他证明，可以通过工程手段使具有微小手性分子失衡的溶液产生手性不断增加的反应产物。这种自我放大可以产生快速变化。例如，仅重复反应三次，Soai博士就能使溶液的不对称性增加63万倍。所谓的Soai反应，并不是生命手性产生的方式。首先，Soai博士使用的试剂在40亿年前不可能存在。但正如一位诺贝尔奖委员会成员所解释的那样，尽管如此，这是自数十亿年前生命诞生以来，人们第一次从非手性分子组合中创造出手性。■

item.title: Burglars could be identified from airborne DNA
item.description:
Science & technology

Science & technology | Every breath you take Oct 8th 2026 BURGLARS HAVE been steadily running out of things they can safely leave behind at a crime scene. First came footprints, then fingerprints and stray fibres. Even microscopic strands of DNA left on tools and surfaces have been used to c...
item.content:encoded:
Burglars could be identified from airborne DNA

Science & technology | Every breath you take

Oct 8th 2026

BURGLARS HAVE been steadily running out of things they can safely leave behind at a crime scene. First came footprints, then fingerprints and stray fibres. Even microscopic strands of DNA left on tools and surfaces have been used to catch the incautious. Now they have something else to worry about: fragments of genetic material in the air.

All people, criminals and non-criminals alike, shed tiny traces of themselves wherever they go. Some of this material—mainly skin cells, dandruff and saliva—ends up suspended as a personal debris cloud that can hang around after the person is gone. A new study published in Forensic Science International: Genetics, a journal, shows that volunteers who pretended to ransack houses in controlled tests could be identified from DNA pulled from the air 30 minutes after they scarpered. As with most forensic evidence, it alone is not proof of wrongdoing. But it could raise some awkward questions for someone without a good reason to be there.

Carried out by a team led by Chiara Fantinato at Oslo University Hospital, the study is an impressive application of methods to capture and analyse what is known as environmental DNA (eDNA)—the genetic traces left by an organism in its surroundings. For more than two decades ecologists have used eDNA from water, soil and atmosphere to detect creatures without needing to see or capture them. The technique has been used to track elusive Burmese pythons in the Florida Everglades and to audit the inhabitants of Loch Ness. (Fish and plenty of eels. No plesiosaurs.)

In 2022 the Oslo group showed that enough eDNA could be collected from indoor air to construct genetic profiles of its occupants. In a separate test, they analysed office air to identify workers who had recently occupied the space. That led them to wonder if the same techniques could be used for forensic purposes. Working with a group in Australia, the researchers found 22 households, split evenly between Oslo and Adelaide, who were willing to allow into their homes first a mock burglar and then a forensics team in full protective gear to run an air-sampling device in the kitchen for a couple of hours.

The intruders were people who had never previously visited the houses. They were asked to spend 15 minutes inside, opening drawers and cupboards as a burglar might. After they fled the scene, the scientists waited 30 minutes, to simulate the delay before investigators might arrive, and then turned on what Dr Fantinato says was basically a vacuum cleaner. They sifted the material collected for DNA and analysed it in the usual way. As airborne DNA falls to the ground, where it contributes to surface dust, the researchers also collected sweeps to build their forensic profiles.

The results offered better news for housebreakers in Australia than Norway. Whereas the samples collected in Oslo could be matched to intruders in 82% of cases, the success rate dropped to 36% for Adelaide. The reasons for the difference are unclear, but could be due to such factors as environmental conditions, the number of people living in the house and how well the various rooms had been cleaned.

There are other complications to note. DNA found in the air does not always have to be from a recent visit, for example: movement can stir DNA-carrying dust into the air, or DNA from people who have never set foot inside could be carried in on people’s clothes. The researchers themselves were surprised by how sensitive their technique was. Despite the efforts they put in to prevent their own DNA leaking into the crime scenes, some was vacuumed up and identified anyway.

It is unlikely, Dr Fantinato says, that air samples would ever prove reliable enough to provide the clinching evidence of someone’s guilt. “It’s an investigative tool,” she says. “Like other types of DNA evidence, it’s just part of the puzzle.” It is still too early to apply the method to real cases. That will require understanding such nuances as why different people shed different amounts of DNA, and standardising techniques between labs. But her team has spoken to police forces about one day helping them with their enquiries. ■

item.content:encoded:
OpenAI声称解决了数百个长期存在的数学难题

科学与技术 | 数字运算 2026年10月8日 2026年10月6日（星期二）可能会成为数学史上最具里程碑意义的日子之一。就在那天，美国人工智能公司OpenAI宣布，其由未发布模型驱动的AI智能体在数周内至少解决了372个长期存在的数学问题。这些发现详细记载于700多篇AI生成的论文中，代表了前所未有的研究规模和速度。这样的成果泛滥让一些人感到不安。对许多研究者而言，发现潜在新数学真理的兴奋感，伴随着对其领域未来的担忧。他们表示，若不加倍谨慎，数学的大规模生产将带来更多解答，却更少理解。

AI在数学领域的进步突飞猛进。就在上个月，OpenAI声称同一个内部模型仅用88小时便解决了纳维-斯托克斯问题——千禧年大奖难题中的标志性问题之一。如今，数百个其他重要难题也被攻克。这些问题覆盖了整个数学体系，从代数、几何到概率论和逻辑学，其中许多已困扰专家数十年。自主数学家们得出一个解答所需的平均算力，仅相当于该公司公开可用模型约三个小时的推理量。尽管其余千禧年大奖难题仍未解决，但其中一两个似乎已取得进展。其中最引人注目的是黎曼猜想，它涉及素数的分布。在这场成果洪流中，还埋葬着一项对棘手难题“三维Kakeya极大猜想”的证明声明。纽约大学库朗研究所的数学家王虹，因在2026年7月的一个密切相关问题上做出贡献而被授予菲尔兹奖——数学界的诺贝尔奖。

究竟取得了哪些突破，以及通过何种手段实现，数学家们可能需要数年时间才能厘清；许多论文篇幅超过100页。在已解决的372个问题中，仅有127个附带了保证逻辑一致性的代码（该领域的规范），而智能体的内部推理过程只公布了其中10个。这372个问题也只是OpenAI向其智能体提出的4000个问题中的一部分，不过公司尚未公布哪些问题超出了其能力范围。这样的透明度将有助于评估该技术的能力与局限。

一些人担心这种做法不利于数学的长期进步。上个月OpenAI解决纳维-斯托克斯问题后不久，28位菲尔兹奖得主发表了一封公开信，警告AI实验室对待数学的方式与该领域的目标相悖。写信者指出，将开放性数学问题作为测试新模型能力的基准，模型制造者有可能过早地关闭探索方向，却没有产生新技术、新问题，最终也没有产生新理解。此后已有超过8000名同行签署了这封信。OpenAI声称已注意到这一点。该公司表示，在筹划如何发布其新发现时，它借鉴了一个独立咨询小组的建议——该小组由九位著名数学家组成，是在纳维-斯托克斯声明发布后成立的。除了分享其模型内部推理的一些细节外，OpenAI还承诺资助一系列会议，以帮助理解这些成果。

总而言之，OpenAI此次发布的规模意味着其真正影响只能事后才能看清。瑞士洛桑联邦理工学院的马丁·海雷尔表示：“一个问题的真正重要性，最终取决于它开辟的新途径以及其证明为其他问题带来的启示。”海雷尔既是OpenAI咨询小组的成员，也是那封菲尔兹奖得主公开信的签署人之一。就目前而言，AI所揭示的数学问题更多是关乎存在性，而非数值性。■

item.title: Should you be using a tongue-scraper?
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Should you be using a tongue-scraper?

Science & technology | Well Informed

Oct 8th 2026

People have used tongue-scrapers since at least the Roman era. Napoleon Bonaparte’s was made of silver. George Washington took his everywhere. Today “influencers” like Hailey Bieber and Gwyneth Paltrow scrape their tongues as part of their “wellness” routines. But does tongue-scraping add anything to dental hygiene that brushing and flossing can’t do alone?

The mouth, like the gut, is home to lots of microbes. A healthy oral microbiome includes around 700 species of bacteria, along with fungi, protozoa and viruses. But poor oral hygiene, smoking or bad diet can upset the balance. That results in bacterial colonies, called biofilms, in which species thrive that cause tooth cavities, gum disease and chronic bad breath (halitosis).

Biofilms are the basis of dental plaque, which forms because teeth, unlike the mouth’s other tissues, are not constantly shedding their cells, and thus any bacteria clinging to them. But tongues, which host about two-thirds of the oral microbiome, are also susceptible to biofilms—which can turn them white or yellow. The gaps between the tiny protuberances covering a tongue’s upper surface teem with bacteria and are especially hospitable to anaerobic species, the respiration of which does not require oxygen but does often generate foul-smelling sulphurous compounds.

Given all this, it might be expected that evidence for the virtues of regular tongue-cleaning would be as abundant as that for cleaning teeth. Alas there is not much.

A trial published in 2018, involving 36 people suffering from gum disease, for example, found that adding tongue scraping to a normal dental-cleaning routine did indeed reduce halitosis. Another, on 45 children, which was published in 2015, showed it significantly lowered levels of Streptococcus mutans—a principal cause of tooth decay.

This particular trial, however, cast doubt on the idea that you need to use a special instrument to keep your tongue clean, for it also found that brushing tongues with a normal toothbrush or rinsing the mouth with salt water both worked just as well as using an actual scraper. Similarly, a third trial—of 56 people with bad breath, published in 2021—found that tongue-scraping and tongue-brushing removed tongue biofilms and reduced odiferous sulphur compounds to the same degree. A fourth, of another 80 bad-breathed individuals, published earlier this year, got similar results with tongue-brushing (rather than scraping) backed up by a dose of Streptococcus salivarius, a so-called oral probiotic that crowds out hostile bacteria such as S. mutans.

Good lingual hygiene may also improve someone’s sense of taste. A review of four trials published in 2025 found that removing tongue coatings increased intensity of salt perception, with one study doing so for 60% of participants.

Together, these results suggest tongue-scrapers might indeed do the biz, but that other approaches to lingual hygiene (including using the toothbrush with which you anyway clean your teeth) can be equally effective. Nevertheless, Zoe Brookes, a professor of dentistry at the University of Plymouth, urges caution. The studies, she says, are too small to draw strong conclusions. And removing too many bacteria from a healthy tongue might equally disrupt the oral microbiome. To maintain a healthy mouth, she observes, nothing beats toothbrushing (twice daily), flossing and cutting out the sweets.■

After a free, evidence-based guide to health and wellness? Sign up to our weekly Well Informed newsletter.

item.description:
Culture

Culture | Pods for demigods Oct 8th 2026 EACH WEEKDAY morning Jordi Hays and John Coogan, two entrepreneurs-turned-podcasters, enter a sauna in Los Angeles with copies of the Wall Street Journal. They come out with jackets, ties and hot takes on the tech news of the day. Then they go on air as h...
item.content:encoded:
Superstar podcasts are Silicon Valley’s way of talking to itself

Culture | Pods for demigods

Oct 8th 2026

EACH WEEKDAY morning Jordi Hays and John Coogan, two entrepreneurs-turned-podcasters, enter a sauna in Los Angeles with copies of the Wall Street Journal. They come out with jackets, ties and hot takes on the tech news of the day. Then they go on air as hosts of the “Technology Business Programming Network” (“TBPN”) podcast, riffing with guests, banging gongs and blowing airhorns. The president of TBPN, Dylan Abruscato, calls it a “variety show” in the vein of a late-night talk show. Silicon Valley laps it up. It is not uncommon to see “TBPN”, rather than CNBC, streaming on the TV screens in tech firms’ offices.

Podcasts are the latest example of a power law in Silicon Valley. Only a few become big hitters. Those that do attract the demigods of tech as guests, making them even more influential. “TBPN” has interviewed Sam Altman of OpenAI and Mark Zuckerberg of Meta. The “All-In” Podcast, hosted by four plutocrats who straddle tech and MAGA politics, held a summit in Los Angeles in September attended by Elon Musk and Jensen Huang. (When Donald Trump phoned Nvidia’s boss on stage during the summit, Mr Huang put the president on speakerphone.) Dwarkesh Patel, a bearded 26-year-old who acts—and looks—like a high priest of AI research, hosts tech bigwigs for hours on the “Dwarkesh Podcast”. So does Lex Fridman, a gravel-voiced computer scientist whose podcast runs longer than some marathons.

All share an in-crowd mystique bordering on incestuousness. In April OpenAI reportedly spent $100m-200m to buy then-18-month-old TBPN (though there was no mention of the affiliation during Mr Altman’s interview). The “All-In” hosts are self-described “besties” with many of their billionaire interviewees. In San Francisco Mr Patel has shared digs with Anthropic’s researchers. They are fascinated by AI, which they talk about with passionate intensity and expertise. They are also an echo chamber, with a tin ear at times to the concerns of the rest of America.

This new podcasting elite reflects a big change in Silicon Valley’s relationship with the media. During the last great investment boom, the dotcom era of the 1990s, publications like Wired were tech-industry gospels. They covered the internet like Rolling Stone wrote about rock’n’roll, says John Battelle, a founding editor of Wired: “We thought we were covering the counterculture.”

But the rise of social media and the growing power and wealth of big tech generated a rift between Silicon Valley and news outlets. Mr Battelle says that parts of the tech establishment started to view traditional media as “anti-American” for questioning the “dominance of the tech hierarchy”. For their part, old media, whose business model has been hurt by the tech giants, sometimes smell of sour grapes. Podcasters, who share their guests’ techno-optimism, provide a friendlier platform.

The watershed came during the 2024 presidential race. Led by Mr Trump, politicians saw the medium as a less filtered way of getting their message out than the press or broadcast TV. “All-In” played a role. Two of its billionaire co-hosts, David Sacks and Chamath Palihapitiya, threw a fundraiser in San Francisco for Mr Trump. Shortly afterwards he appeared on their show. That helped raise the profile of the hosts, as well as of tech podcasting in general. (For more than a year Mr Sacks was Mr Trump’s AI “czar”, even dressing the part by wearing a Russian fur hat at an “All-In” event.)

Since then such superstar shows have gone from strength to strength. They take different approaches. The hosts of “All-In” delight in being anti-woke. They abhor what they call the “lamestream media” almost as much as they lampoon effective altruism (EA), a philosophical doctrine that they argue puts too much focus on the existential risks of AI. Mr Patel, in contrast, has said EA influenced him to start the “Dwarkesh Podcast” on ai. “TBPN” is not all bells and whistles. Its hosts have a deep knowledge of venture capital (VC), which they demystify with quips; they also work closely with media outlets and give airtime to their tech scoops.

Helping them thrive is what would be called, in Silicon Valley jargon, a flywheel. Just before he hit the big time in 2024, Mr Patel tweeted his bank balance. It showed savings of $0.14. Then Mr Zuckerberg came onto the show and the advertising dollars poured in. As more prominent executives take part, not only do advertisers notice; so do potential customers, investors and jobseekers, raising the quality of the audience. “This is luxurious media with very valuable eyeballs,” says Josh Kaplan, boss of Smooth Media, which represents podcasters.

The format is particularly well-suited to Silicon Valley, where founders invent stories for a living. They are venerated like the great men of history (Silicon Valley is still mostly a great manosphere). “We’re not journalists; we are enthusiasts,” says Patrick O’Shaughnessy, whose podcast, “Invest Like the Best”, has a strong following in VC circles. Firms such as Andreessen Horowitz have piled in too, creating podcasts to tout their portfolio companies to investors and themselves to founders. These offerings may be popular, but do not expect them to invest in the costly investigative work that uncovers frauds, such as that at Theranos, a health-tech startup, exposed by the Wall Street Journal in 2015.

Instead, AI is at the centre of their discussions. Unlike many parts of America, they treat it as almost the only topic worth discussing. But this obsession has further pushed Silicon Valley into a “monoculture”, says David Senra, an influential podcaster. Recently he has been to tech dinners where conversation veers only between AI optimism and doomerism. “It sounds like they are all reading the same tweets,” he says.

Lulu Cheng Meservey, a PR consultant to tech founders, reckons nine-tenths of people in tech speak only to other people in tech. Podcasts exacerbate that. As for using the format to transmit enthusiasm about AI to the outside world, it is not working. They may be well-meaning, she says, but “when a billionaire AI salesman is telling you whether to buy AI, you are taking that from someone who is entirely unrelatable to you.”

It may get worse. Silicon Valley’s podcasters sprinkle their conversations with reverence for space missions, robots and other techno-wizardry. In an AIpocalypse, they would come out better off than most people. Mr Battelle calls it the “golden ticket on the rocket ship”. If all else fails, they can podcast from Mars. But will people still want to listen to them? ■

item.title: “The Social Reckoning” is a fatally earnest sequel to a classic
item.description:
Culture

Culture | Film Oct 8th 2026 “I’m not two years out of a dorm room anymore,” snaps Mark Zuckerberg at an adviser in “The Social Reckoning”. The last time Facebook’s boss was portrayed on the big screen, a dorm is precisely where he was. “The Social Network” (2010) dramatised the company’s birth a...
item.content:encoded:
“The Social Reckoning” is a fatally earnest sequel to a classic

Culture | Film

Oct 8th 2026

“I’m not two years out of a dorm room anymore,” snaps Mark Zuckerberg at an adviser in “The Social Reckoning”. The last time Facebook’s boss was portrayed on the big screen, a dorm is precisely where he was. “The Social Network” (2010) dramatised the company’s birth at Harvard and established Mr Zuckerberg’s reputation as a chilly, ruthless weirdo. Its epilogue noted that Facebook had 500m members and that Mr Zuckerberg was the world’s youngest billionaire. Today Facebook has 3bn users and its 42-year-old boss is worth a quarter of a trillion dollars.

“The Social Reckoning”, a much-anticipated sequel to “The Social Network”, takes place around 15 years later. It follows Jeff Horwitz, a journalist at the Wall Street Journal (played by Jeremy Allen White), as he coaxes information from Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison), a disillusioned member of Facebook’s toothless “Civic Integrity Team”. The film adopts its predecessor’s time-hopping structure, flipping between hunts for the material and publication, when all hell breaks loose.

The movies share a writer in the form of Aaron Sorkin, who won an Oscar for his “Social Network” script (which was based on a book). But there the similarities end. Mr Sorkin stood in for the original director, David Fincher. Jesse Eisenberg declined to play Mr Zuckerberg for a second time, so the role has gone to Jeremy Strong, best known for “Succession”.

The main problem with “The Social Reckoning” is not that its director or actors have changed. It is that Facebook itself has. Back in 2010 Facebook was cool. It had been available to the general public for only four years: young people were glued to it; their grandparents had not yet taken it over. Mr Zuckerberg, then 26, was Time’s person of the year. “The Social Network” was devastating because it methodically gutted the world’s hottest company and its founder (or rather, co-founder, as the film made clear).

Today’s Facebook is a mightier company but a softer target. Social networks are reviled by legislators, litigators and parents. Facebook and its rivals have paid out in multiple court cases involving harm to children. Its efforts to silence criticism—gagging a former executive who wrote a book, “Careless People”, for instance—have backfired spectacularly. Almost no one in the world is less cool than Mr Zuckerberg, whose approval rating in America is -43%, just ahead of Vladimir Putin.

The result is that “The Social Reckoning”, which styles itself as an exposé, often feels more like a sermon for the converted. Mr Strong, who is known for his extreme method-acting approach, has nailed Mr Zuckerberg’s monotone voice and stiff manner. But whereas the young Zuck of “The Social Network” was a complex character—arrogant and treacherous but tragically insecure—in the “Reckoning” he is a cartoon villain. Surrounded by computer monitors and a bulletproof sofa in his imperial headquarters, he barks at quivering underlings as they labour through their slide decks. “Fuckin’ Civic Integrity”, he scoffs, after the team meekly suggests dialling down harmful content at the expense of 1% of engagement.

His henchmen are no subtler. Facebook’s comically horrid PR man says that the social network is better than any nation. “We’re post-government around here,” he sneers, when threatened with regulation. The now-familiar notion that the company puts profit before the greater good is conveyed with a megaphone. “If engagement keeps falling…it’ll be a bad earnings report!” squeals one executive, as the company debates whether to tone down its wickedness.

The second difficulty for the movie is that its subject matter is more nuanced than Mr Sorkin would like. The film’s central question—should Facebook suppress bad content?—is not so simple. The script implies that Facebook should take down lies. But should the flawed Mr Zuckerberg therefore be elevated to a global arbiter of truth? Some dialogue is unintentionally persuasive to the contrary. “The voters aren’t children,” argues Mr Zuckerberg in one scene. “Facebook isn’t the ref…We’re the public square.” Quite.

Mr Sorkin’s earnestness was perfectly tempered by Mr Fincher’s cynicism in “The Social Network”. It was a movie with no real heroes, between the perfidious Mr Zuckerberg and those he trampled, including a flash Sean Parker (an early supporter) and the absurd Winklevoss twins (who say Mr Zuckerberg stole their idea). The “Reckoning”, by contrast, is divided neatly into goodies (diligent journalist, brave whistleblower) and baddies (scheming Zuckerberg, robotic cronies). The outcome is an unsatisfying caricature.

Film and TV schedules have lately been clogged with dramatisations of Silicon Valley. The most successful ones have tended to be those based on true stories, including what happened at Uber (“Super Pumped”), WeWork (“WeCrashed”) and Theranos (“The Dropout”). But now those corporate dramas are well-known—and helped make up people’s minds about the Valley’s recklessness.

Yet more takes are on the way. On October 8th Paramount+ will launch “Cupertino”, a series about a fictional law firm fighting big tech. A new documentary about Theranos’s Elizabeth Holmes will come out this month, too. In December “Artificial”, starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman, will be the first movie to tell the story of OpenAI. “The Social Network” remains the model for how to do it well. Alas, its follow-up offers a reminder of what a hard act it is to follow. ■

item.title: Malcolm Gladwell and Harel Shapira are up in arms about guns
item.description:
Culture

Culture | Under the gun Oct 8th 2026 FEW THINGS about Americans baffle foreigners more than their attachment to guns. Thirty years ago mass shootings in Australia and Scotland prompted both countries to tighten their gun laws; today, legally owning a handgun in Britain is almost impossible and g...
item.content:encoded:
Malcolm Gladwell and Harel Shapira are up in arms about guns

Culture | Under the gun

Oct 8th 2026

FEW THINGS about Americans baffle foreigners more than their attachment to guns. Thirty years ago mass shootings in Australia and Scotland prompted both countries to tighten their gun laws; today, legally owning a handgun in Britain is almost impossible and getting one in Australia requires licensing, registration and a background check. In America, meanwhile, 40% of people live in a household with a gun, and each year more than 1m Americans become first-time gun owners. What explains this form of American exceptionalism? Two new books try to answer that question in very different ways.

Malcolm Gladwell, a prolific Canadian journalist who lives in America, has written a book that follows his familiar formula: ten short chapters crammed with anecdotes wrapped around nuggets of wisdom, like social-science fortune cookies. “The American Way of Killing” emerged from a series on his popular podcast, “Revisionist History”; annoyingly, it reads like it, with whole chunks of raw transcript slapped down on the page.

But, as with most of Mr Gladwell’s books, readers will come away thinking differently about the world. For instance, one of the few gun-control measures most Americans support is a ban on assault weapons. Mr Gladwell argues it would do little; most gun deaths involve handguns, which are readily available. Many on the American left would be happy to shrink police forces; Mr Gladwell notes that European cities tend to have larger police forces than similarly sized American ones and argues that keeps them safe, because their presence helps prevent crimes.

Mr Gladwell’s usually fluid writing has a shrill, rebarbative edge. He accuses Americans of “moral recklessness”, misdiagnosing “the nature of the violence that plagues their streets” and having a “fundamentally dishonest way” of discussing guns. “Not only do Americans get things wrong, but they seem uninterested in ever getting things right,” he huffs. Those who share his views on guns may enjoy his scolding, but his tone will turn some off.

Harel Shapira, by contrast, does far more showing than telling. A sociologist at the University of Texas, Mr Shapira spent years taking firearms-training classes in Texas to better understand why and how guns appeal to ordinary Americans. The instructors are dedicated professionals, mostly conservative but not nutters “running tactical drills deep in the woods in preparation for a battle with the deep state”. Both students and instructors sincerely believe that owning and knowing how to use guns will help keep them safer.

Mr Shapira and his fellow students do not just learn to load, aim and clean their weapons. They are also taught “the ‘warrior mindset’" or “the state of mind that we ‘good guys with guns’ were meant to embrace”. The school’s founder says that there are three types of people: sheep (passive), wolves (predatory) and the type he wants them to be: sheepdogs, who protect the flock. The police are a “reactive force” who often arrive too late; a sheepdog has to always be prepared for danger.

The school’s founder encourages them to carry their guns loaded. “There are bad guys everywhere,” he warns. Many of Mr Shapira’s fellow students fear petrol stations, where they feel vulnerable when they get out of their cars to refuel. For his instructors, Mr Shapira writes, “a diverse and vibrant public sphere does not hold the promise of a fulfilling life. It holds only the potential for a violent death.”

The consequences of a mindset that encourages an armed response to ubiquitous danger quickly becomes clear. One of his instructors shot and killed a young black man who broke into his home. It turned out he was a mentally disabled resident of a nearby group home who had escaped and ran down the street, banging on front doors. When the young man, dishevelled and probably “cold, frightened, disoriented”, did not heed the instructor’s orders to leave, he shot him five times.

Was the instructor a “good guy with a gun”? Some thought so: he faced no charges. Mr Shapira is not so sure. But what makes his book so exceptional is that his personal doubts did not stop him from listening to his instructor’s story with empathy, curiosity and understanding—all of which he extends to his subjects.

In that sense, these two books are not just about guns; they present two ways of engaging in culture-war arguments. Both authors dislike guns and presumably wrote their books to persuade others of their beliefs. Mr Gladwell tries to scold his opponents into submission, which seldom works. Mr Shapira, however, listens and shows his readers a world full of complex people rather than caricatures.

Whether any author can change minds on this issue is a bleaker question. A majority of American adults has been threatened with a gun, seen someone shot or had a family member killed by a gun, according to KFF, a think-tank. Yet in recent years American gun laws have become only laxer, with states embracing “permitless carry” of firearms. America’s gun-violence problem will last until voters follow Australians and Britons—and decide they have had enough. ■

item.content:encoded:
想穿越中东一游吗？

文化 | 夹在中间的男人 2026年10月8日

据某些说法，那是史上最昂贵的派对。为纪念波斯帝国建立2500周年，伊朗末代国王穆罕默德·礼萨·巴列维邀请各国国王、王后、皇帝和总统，在波斯波利斯古城废墟间的一处奢华营地中共同庆祝。宾客们啜饮酩悦香槟和拉菲罗斯柴尔德酒庄的葡萄酒，享用来自巴黎马克西姆餐厅的美食，还对着5万只进口鸣禽目瞪口呆。（这些鸟儿最终全部死于酷热。）伊朗民众对这种奢靡感到愤怒。“我们几乎连面包和萝卜都供不起他们，”国王如此麻木不仁地回怼道。对于伊朗革命的缔造者与精神之父阿亚图拉鲁霍拉·霍梅尼而言，这场派对是“魔鬼的盛宴”。它标志着国王统治终结的开端。七年后，国王出逃国外，亲信被处决，甚至连他的马也遭到公开折磨并被枪杀。派对结束了。

英国历史学家西蒙·塞巴格·蒙蒂菲奥里在上一本书中探讨了世界历史。他的最新著作《大锅》则更加雄心勃勃：它梳理了自1900年以来中东的历史。你可能会想，这个主题还有什么新东西可说？关于阿拉伯人的厚重历史著作比比皆是。以色列人与巴勒斯坦人之间的冲突，用蒙蒂菲奥里自己的话说，已经催生了“一个名副其实的产业”的分析。无数大部头梳理了塑造该地区的外交、战争与革命。

蒙蒂菲奥里的贡献在多个方面独树一帜。他涵盖了整个中东核心地带，包括土耳其、伊朗、以色列和阿拉伯国家：这是一种出奇罕见的做法。更重要的是，他将读者带至当下，分析仍在持续展开的事件。他旨在通过“人的故事，往往是统治者的故事”来讲述这段历史，从而“为宗教、地缘政治和意识形态的沉重议题增添轻盈”。蒙蒂菲奥里还希望为西方人看待中东的方式“恢复某种平衡”。这些任务无一轻松。

然而，《大锅》的宏大视野令人叹为观止。他在该地区飞速穿梭，从1915年穆斯塔法·凯末尔·阿塔图尔克与协约国军队作战，到1932年阿卜杜勒阿齐兹·本·阿卜杜勒·拉赫曼·沙特夺取利雅得、建立沙特王国。随后，这本书继续推进，历经以色列建国、伊朗革命、苏丹内战的恐怖以及过去三年的血腥冲突。

书的广度不可避免地意味着深度的牺牲。1915-16年的亚美尼亚种族灭绝仅用不到一页篇幅处理。但蒙蒂菲奥里也成功纳入了大量细节，使宏大叙事栩栩如生（例如，伊朗是继美国之后第二个承认新以色列国的国家；或者埃及的贾迈勒·阿卜杜勒·纳赛尔对列昂尼德·勃列日涅夫说，如果他是以色列领导人：“我绝不会放弃被占领土。”）。

鉴于蒙蒂菲奥里匆匆掠过如此多的“人的故事”，他或许本可以借鉴吉莉·库珀女爵士某部作品的做法，附上人物表。那肯定会色彩斑斓。《大锅》中人物纷呈，包括被中情局昵称为“肥混蛋”的埃及国王法鲁克；“穿着睡衣的病秧子”穆罕默德·摩萨台；以及新伊朗共和国首任总统阿布哈桑·巴尼萨德尔，他有着“滑稽的小胡子、过大的眼镜和法国新浪潮电影导演式的利落西装”。

平衡则更为棘手。他首先通过该地区各成员国的视角直接书写，而非从帝国主义者或入侵者的角度切入。在美国正逐步退出其作为中东主导力量的角色、且没有哪个国家显得愿意或能够接替之际，这是一种值得的努力。

在历史仍在形成之际书写历史尤为困难。他对2023年10月7日袭击事件及以色列回应——“其历史上规模最大、时间最长、最不受约束的战争”——的分析，在许多读者看来极为合理。然而，毫无疑问，一些人会认为他的判断对以色列过于宽容，而另一些读者则认为他对巴勒斯坦人过于同情。但他真正精准之处在于他对伊朗革命重要性的强调。他将伊朗编织进中东历史之中，而非像许多其他人那样孤立地对待它，并突出其对地区乃至世界的重要性，这是本书的显著成就之一。他将伊朗革命的影响比作1789年法国大革命和1917年俄国革命，认为与它们一样，它“改变了世界”。当前中东的乱局印证了这一判断。■

item.title: 为什么你最喜欢的面包店和咖啡店现在都开始卖帆布手提袋了
item.description:
Culture

文化 | 着装密码 2026年10月8日 从郁金香和兰花到豆宝宝玩偶和宝可梦卡片，人类对狂热痴迷并不陌生。但最奇怪的现象之一，莫过于当下对美国杂货店Trader Joe's迷你手提袋的追捧。9月30日推出的限时万圣节主题手提袋——售价2.99美元，大小与iPad相当——引发了全美各地门店外的长队。一些Trader Joe's门店对每位顾客可购买的数量实施了严格限制。（人们似乎并不介意这些手提袋小到没什么实际用处。）狂热爱好者们转而涌向转售网站，售价在20美元到异想天开的5万美元之间。 周边商品——用时髦的说法叫“merch”——似乎无处不在，适用于一切事物。研究公司牛津经济研究院估计，全球每...
item.content:encoded:
为什么你最喜欢的面包店和咖啡店现在都开始卖帆布手提袋了

文化 | 着装密码 2026年10月8日

从郁金香和兰花到豆宝宝玩偶和宝可梦卡片，人类对狂热痴迷并不陌生。但最奇怪的现象之一，莫过于当下对美国杂货店Trader Joe's迷你手提袋的追捧。9月30日推出的限时万圣节主题手提袋——售价2.99美元，大小与iPad相当——引发了全美各地门店外的长队。一些Trader Joe's门店对每位顾客可购买的数量实施了严格限制。（人们似乎并不介意这些手提袋小到没什么实际用处。）狂热爱好者们转而涌向转售网站，售价在20美元到异想天开的5万美元之间。

周边商品——用时髦的说法叫“merch”——似乎无处不在，适用于一切事物。研究公司牛津经济研究院估计，全球每年在这方面花费3380亿美元。（他们相当宽泛的定义包括授权产品、服装、品牌商品和按需印刷产品。）从面包店、书店到家喻户晓的品牌和五金店，各种公司都在兜售此类商品。就连科技公司也加入了进来。Palantir在7月推出了带有其标志的白色网球服。最近OpenAI发布了其首个公开发售的服装系列。“这是在大庭广众之下被霸凌的最佳方式，”一位X用户嘲讽道。

当然，周边商品并不是什么新鲜事。长期以来，它在三个领域一直很常见。一个是儿童产品——任何不得不为一条艾莎裙或巴斯光年玩具掏钱的家长都深有体会。另一个领域是音乐。巴克莱银行预测，哈里·斯泰尔斯的粉丝们今年夏天在该歌手巡演的伦敦站每人将挥霍100英镑（约合135美元）。周边商品也是体育队的一大收入来源。纽约仍然到处是蓝橙配色的服饰，这是尼克斯队的颜色，该队是纽约市获胜的篮球队。英超球队阿森纳在2024-25赛季的球衣和周边商品收入增长了26%，达到1.3亿英镑。

然而如今，更多种类的企业正在把周边商品当作营销手段。制作这类产品既便宜又容易，这有所帮助。一个帆布手提袋批量生产可能成本不到1美元，但在其使用寿命期间可能会被成千上万人看到。对于Daunt Books或莎士比亚书店——它们的帆布手提袋深受文人喜爱——这意味着数十亿次的曝光。周边商品还能让公司展现有趣的形象。许多公司借助幽默来传达个性。6月，超市Lidl配合世界杯推出了“三只Lidl球衣”。这款恶搞的英格兰足球衣采用防液体和防异味面料：这样更能承受周围热情球迷喷洒的啤酒。它在55秒内售罄。

对消费者来说，品牌周边可以是支持心爱本地企业的一种方式，这一趋势在疫情期间得到推动。纽约大学的贾里德·沃森表示，周边商品热潮也标志着年轻人通过衣着和配饰进行“信号传递”的方式发生了变化。他说，在数字时代长大改变了他们的消费心理。服装品牌看起来千篇一律。现在，人们渴望通过自己经历过的体验或去过的地方来展示个性，这些让他们感觉自己与众不同。“地位的形式已经改变，”品牌咨询公司Tracksuit的康纳·阿奇博尔德表示：“过去你用价格标签、设计师品牌或昂贵的手表来彰显地位。现在更多是看品味和归属感。”

与直觉相反，穿周边商品来脱颖而出也是一种与社群建立联系的方式。西方近一半的公民不隶属于任何组织，无论是信仰团体、体育俱乐部还是其他公民组织。在这种社会原子化的背景下，穿一件周边商品——尤其是某个小众事物的周边——就相当于“在大池塘里当一条小鱼，还能找到其他小鱼”，沃森先生说。对一些人来说，终极目标仅仅是得到陌生人会心的赞许点头。

下一个趋势是更具个人化的周边商品。像Etsy这样的公司让消费者能够生产定制物品，如杯子、火柴和T恤，用作生日派对、单身派对和婚礼的回礼。今年，《建筑文摘》报道了人们送给房客周边商品的事，并问道：“你的家应该有自己的周边商品吗？”人们越珍视体验，纪念品就越有价值。大家都明白了这一点。■

item.title: Cyril Hilsum invented the flat-screen displays that hold us in thrall
item.description:
Obituary

Obituary | The world seen anew Oct 8th 2026 Whenever in later life a fresh idea struck him, Cyril Hilsum would leave the dinner table and wander to his lab. He didn’t have far to go. Part of it was in the garage, part in the scullery, of his house in Pinner, north-west of London. The rest was in...
item.content:encoded:
Cyril Hilsum invented the flat-screen displays that hold us in thrall

Obituary | The world seen anew

Oct 8th 2026

Whenever in later life a fresh idea struck him, Cyril Hilsum would leave the dinner table and wander to his lab. He didn’t have far to go. Part of it was in the garage, part in the scullery, of his house in Pinner, north-west of London. The rest was in the kitchen. One counter was his electronics bench, with an oscilloscope, a pair of waveform generators, a spectrum analyser and a tray of voltage dividers looped to each other and to a soldering station with a maze of cables. On the facing counter stood a three-roll mill for working conductive powders, a precision balance, a small vacuum chamber and many labelled jars of carbon black and nickel powder. Everything had its place here apart from kitchen stuff; but he dined, and lunched too, mostly on red wine, ready meals and chocolate. Fruit and veg he disdained. He lived very healthily on a diet of curiosity, hard work and endless ideas.

In all he had over 70 patents to his name. The last, filed when he was 97, was for ink with sensors that conducted electricity. His lasting fame, though, came from liquid-crystal displays. In the 1970s he realised that these could replace the bulky, power-hungry TVs of old, with their bulging cathode-ray tubes and curved screens, with slim flat-screen models that could be hung on a wall. He and his collaborators started small, with digital watches in 1974; but in no time flat screens were everywhere, in computer monitors, cockpit displays, departure boards and, especially, mobile phones. Sharper images took longer; but in the modern screen-bound age, he changed the world’s way of seeing.

It had been difficult work. Liquid crystals certainly behaved like liquids, because they flowed, but their molecules could keep a structure for a very brief time. It was up to him to stabilise them and induce them to work at room temperature. In two years he and two colleagues, George Gray and Peter Raynes, produced and patented a whole new controllable family of them.

His second-proudest achievement was to build in 1962 Britain’s first semiconductor laser, which involved getting gallium arsenide to behave. This was extremely hard. To make it he had to mix gallium with arsenic in a silica tube, heat it furiously, stick it in a shed and wait til morning. By then it would have burst the tube asunder, and he would have to pick out the pieces. But now he had a compound whose electrons were finely tuned to convert electrical energy efficiently into light, making a laser so compact that it could be used with ordinary batteries in everyday devices: CD players, burglar alarms, speed-detection devices, LEDs, printers and scanners.

The mini-radars proved especially useful. They could be fitted under trains to start them braking, even at 200mph, and one version, called Claribel, used the speed and trajectory of a bullet to pinpoint the position of hidden snipers in Northern Ireland. Once deployed, the sniping stopped. As for him he was stopped too, by a policeman with a speed-gun, as he roared down a motorway in his usual mode; but got away with it by saying he was its inventor, and that one was wrongly calibrated. He didn’t lose many arguments, even with the law. But then, with his nimbus of hair and his high domed forehead, he did look every inch an inventor.

At that time he was working at the Royal Signals and Radar Establishment at Malvern, where he stayed from 1964 to 1983. Strictly speaking he was a civil servant, although he never felt like one; he was a scientist and an engineer. An engineer first perhaps, who at three had taken his toys apart to see how they worked and, sometimes, succeeded in reassembling them. His bent was practical and, often, commercial. That came from being the son of struggling street traders in the East End. At weekends he worked on the stalls (chamois leather on Portobello Road, flat caps on Petticoat Lane), and in the evenings he often watched his father concealing, with gold paint, the printed price on chocolate bars, in order to sell them for more. A large part of his impetus to replace cathode-ray tubes was the fact that the British government was paying huge royalties to the Radio Corporation of America for using them. When everyone went roaring after liquid crystals, the government speedily earned £100m.

He was still frustrated, though, by officialdom’s general failure to exploit the good ideas British scientists had, and at 57 he left Malvern to lead the GEC Hirst Research Centre. Amazingly, it was the first time he had ever decided what to do in life. Previously, he had simply moved from project to project as ministers or higher-ups dictated. He went willingly, because every promotion was a step further from the East End, and because his quick mind (he beat Alan Turing at chess, once) always won him a measure of independence. At school he and his friend Jack had been allowed to sit in the back row, working at their own fast pace. At both Malvern and at GEC, and before that, he had a lab of his own.

He believed strongly, however, that scientists should be accountable for what they were doing. His consistent question was, Why? Why had his mother insisted on washing him every day, when he hardly got dirty? And why did theoretical physicists sit every day at their desks or in their labs, enjoying taxpayer funding, without trying to apply what they had learned? If they had seen an effect, it was up to them to find a use for it, as he infallibly had.

In 2006 the British Liquid Crystal Society introduced a Cyril Hilsum medal. He was pleased, but almost embarassed. He cared more about the scholarship he had set up in memory of his wife Betty, his rock, and the prize he started in memory of his daughter Karen, who died at 42. She had been a promising engineer. All through his career he had hired or promoted women equally with men. In fact, as scientists he preferred them. Men cared about learning more; women cared about using science for good. That was much more crucial, for him, than any wonders they might do in the kitchen. And anyway, they could hardly get into his. ■

item.content:encoded:
政治

本周要闻 2026年10月1日

唐纳德·特朗普拒绝了伊朗提出的一项协议，该协议提议如果美国解除对伊朗港口的封锁，伊朗将在七天内重新向商业船只开放霍尔木兹海峡，并恢复核谈判。他告诉助手们，他预计将在11月中期选举后再次开始轰炸伊朗。特朗普先生表示，美国对该海峡拥有“完全控制权”，并且“大量石油”正从中通过。

最后一批美国和英国军队离开伊拉克，结束了他们自2014年以来在该国的存在。当年他们作为国际联盟的一部分被派往那里，打击圣战组织“伊斯兰国”。伊拉克总理表示，他们的撤离预示着伊拉克将转向“对其安全与稳定承担全部责任”。

一架从迪拜飞往特拉维夫的迪拜航空航班在副驾驶刺伤机长后，不到两分钟内骤降近两万英尺并发出求救信号，随后改道飞往沙特阿拉伯。以色列国防部长以色列·卡茨声称，初步证据表明这名失控飞行员意图让飞机坠毁，杀死机上所有人，并将其称为“一次未遂的圣战恐怖袭击”。乘客们制服了袭击者，使其他飞行员得以将飞机降落。以色列总理本雅明·内塔尼亚胡称赞这位印度机长奋起反抗，是“真正的英雄”。

法蒂玛·扎赫拉·曼苏里被任命为摩洛哥首位女总理，此前她的自由党在最近的议会选举中赢得最多席位。国王穆罕默德六世选择了曾任马拉喀什市长的曼苏里女士，而非她的党内同事、足协主席福齐·莱克贾。

非洲首富阿利科·丹格特和肯尼亚总统威廉·鲁托在肯尼亚沿海的拉穆为一所耗资160亿美元的炼油厂奠基，他们希望这将降低东非的燃料成本和精炼产品进口费用。埃塞俄比亚总理阿比·艾哈迈德、乌干达总统约韦里·穆塞韦尼以及其他几位非洲领导人出席了仪式。丹格特先生已在祖国尼日利亚运营一家大型炼油厂。

几内亚比绍前总统乌马罗·西索科·恩巴洛在2025年11月的政变中被推翻，他表示将回国参加12月6日的总统选举。这一声明加剧了人们的怀疑，认为恩巴洛先生策划了这场政变——政变发生在他预计将败选的选举结果公布前夕。

特朗普先生与习近平的峰会没有取得重大突破，尽管中美两国确实同意各自削减对对方价值300亿美元商品的关税（不包括大豆），并表示将建立美中超级智能对话（中方称之为人工智能对话）。这将包括一个报告人工智能事件的机制。

英国军情五处情报机构警告英国学者，北京的中国通用技术研究院与中国情报机构有密切联系，并正在资助有助于中国间谍活动的研究。军情五处表示，学者们可能不知道这些联系，但敦促大学切断与该研究院的关系，并称如果不这样做，他们可能违反国家安全法。

马来西亚开始将首批5000名寻求庇护者遣返缅甸，这是它与缅甸军政府协调制定的一项计划的一部分。来自缅甸罗兴亚穆斯林群体的难民在马来西亚遭遇了一波敌意，面临被强行逐出村庄和学校的处境。据信该国约有12.6万名罗兴亚人。政府坚称遣返是自愿的，但联合国人员被禁止对他们进行筛查。目前尚不清楚首批离开的难民中是否有罗兴亚人。

在缅甸，据报道至少有50人在靠近孟加拉国边境的皎道镇的一次空袭中丧生。此次空袭是缅甸武装部队对若开军的最新攻势，若开军是一个分离主义组织，也对罗兴亚人犯下了暴行。

泰国的洪水死亡人数升至23人。曼谷在三天内遭遇了32厘米（12.6英寸）的降雨，导致其主要机场运营受阻。市中心的水位开始消退，但外围郊区预计需要更长时间排干。预计首都很快还会有更多强降雨。

乌克兰基辅的国家科学院在俄罗斯对首都的又一次空袭中被无人机击中。至少两人在科学院丧生。该科学院成立于1918年，负责协调乌克兰主要机构的研究工作。

英国反恐警方表示，在五名最初被怀疑企图袭击费尔福德空军基地的男子的货车中未发现爆炸装置。美国轰炸机从该基地起飞，执行打击伊朗军事设施的任务。在这五人被捕后，英国政府召开了紧急COBRA安全会议，但尽管官方怀疑伊朗介入，他们仍被保释，等待进一步调查。

于7月接任英国首相的安迪·伯纳姆在利物浦的工党会议上发表了重要演讲。民调支持率上升的伯纳姆先生传达了“再次充满希望”的信息，并表示他希望为十年的分裂画上句号。他承诺解决三个棘手问题：国家养老金、选举制度和欧洲，尽管这些改革被推迟到下一次大选之后，而下一次大选要到2029年才举行（伯纳姆先生确实宣布成立一个全国委员会来研究选举改革）。工党的反对者表示，他的演讲对解决英国今天面临的问题毫无帮助。

在法国，明年总统选举中领先的中右翼候选人爱德华·菲利普概述了一项养老金改革计划，拟将最低退休年龄从接近63岁提高到65岁。菲利普先生称法国相对较低的退休年龄是不可持续的，并表示如果不进行改革，就有爆发金融危机的风险。最新统计数据显示，公共债务再次上升，达到GDP的119%。法国的主权借贷成本升至2008年以来的最高水平。政府公布了2027年预算，承诺节省540亿欧元（610亿美元）。但它表示赤字将占GDP的5%，远高于欧盟3%的上限。

田纳西州200年来首位面临死刑的女性在执行注射死刑后活了下来。克里斯塔·派克于1996年被判谋杀同学罪，当时她18岁。在行刑失败后，她被转移到一家医疗机构。监狱管理局坚称遵循了适当程序，并称已为她注射了两针致命注射化学药剂。

巴西总统竞选候选人进入10月4日大选前的最后竞选阶段。左翼现任总统路易斯·伊纳西奥·卢拉·达席尔瓦对保守派挑战者弗拉维奥·博尔索纳罗保持微弱领先，但在预计于10月25日举行的决选中，这一优势缩小到统计上的平局。

阿根廷总统哈维尔·米莱在社交媒体上就福克兰群岛大发雷霆，并威胁说，除非一项英以石油勘探项目在两周内停止运营，否则将对该项目采取法律行动。米莱先生称该项目对阿根廷构成“明确而现实的危险”。他最近还抨击联合国未推进阿根廷对该英国领土的主权主张，称联合国“毫无用处”，充斥着“伪装成善意官僚的傲慢寄生虫”。

item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Business

The world this week

Oct 1st 2026

Details emerged about Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, which it has circulated among key investors. According to Reuters, revenue at the firm reportedly rose to $4.6bn last year, and it recorded a net loss of $42bn, $34bn of which was an accounting charge. It aims to spend $518bn in the near future on cloud infrastructure and other investments. Anthropic could be valued at $2trn when it lists on the stock market, which would smash the record $1.8trn valuation set by SpaceX only in June. The IPO is not expected until after America’s midterm elections in November. It counted “existential risks to humanity” among the hazards facing its business.

Sam Altman, the boss of OpenAI, said his firm’s already-delayed IPO would not take place until it had tackled concerns about the safety of its technology. OpenAI confirmed that it had withheld the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, after its new model displayed high levels of deception during internal tests. It also suspended trials of other models. The firm has admitted that its agents breached dozens of systems, including some governmental ones.

Confronting worries about AI safety, Nvidia launched an Open Agent Safety Platform that allows companies to track the activities of their AI agents. Jensen Huang, the chipmaker’s boss, is less concerned about the threat from AI to humanity than his fellow tech titans, saying recently that it is up to AI companies to ensure their models are safe and under control. Meanwhile, Nvidia expanded its share buy-back programme by $150bn, taking its total buy-back plan to $235bn, the biggest-ever in corporate America.

AMD struck an agreement to acquire World Labs, a startup, in an $8.2bn deal. World Labs was co-founded by Fei-Fei Li, a leading AI researcher and professor at Stanford University, to develop spatial models that investigate how the three-dimensional physical world works for application in areas such as robotics and gaming. AMD’s acquisition is the latest instance of a chipmaker evolving its business towards the development of advanced AI frontier models.

The sell-off in bond markets continued. The yield on ten-year US Treasuries was over 5.3%, its highest level since 2002. British 30-year gilts crossed 6% and French spreads over German Bunds were back to euro-crisis levels. Donald Trump didn’t help by renewing his call for Jerome Powell to step down from the board of governors at the Federal Reserve, which revived fears about the independence of the central bank and the direction of inflation.

Shein’s first earnings report since listing on the stock market in early September disappointed investors. Adjusted net profit fell by 67%, year on year, and revenue was virtually flat. The ultra-cheap retailer’s share price plunged after it announced its results, giving it a market value of around $17bn, down from $26bn at its IPO.

The German government was reportedly seeking assurances from UniCredit, an Italian bank, about its commitments in any takeover of Commerzbank, Germany’s second-biggest lender, such as keeping its listing in Frankfurt. The government has so far resisted UniCredit’s advances on Commerzbank, but has moderated its opposition to a deal. The Italians are preparing to take control as early as January next year, according to reports, and plan a big restructuring of the bank, including ditching some international business.

Tata Trusts, the charitable group which owns 66% of Tata Sons, proposed merging the holding company with two subsidiaries to avoid a forced public listing. The proposal, led by Noel Tata, a scion of the Tata family, challenges the board’s recent decision to proceed with an IPO.

SpaceX’s Starship rocket marked a milestone by reaching orbit for the first time, despite a failure in one of its three main engines, which cut short its flying time. The mission deployed 26 next-generation Starlink V3 satellites, which increase capacity and data density for Starlink’s broadband service.

Walmart promised its customers that it would not use AI to “set different prices based on who you are or the time of day”. The supermarket chain was responding to concerns about the prospect of retailers using AI to determine a price based on a shopper’s individual data. The Federal Trade Commission has warned recently that businesses that don’t tell consumers their data is being used this way may be breaking the law. Dynamic pricing has long been in use, but now McDonald’s and other fast-food chains are reportedly experimenting with sophisticated algorithms to decide prices based on local demand, so a Big Mac could cost more in one outlet than another nearby.

item.content:encoded:
有效利他主义是本世纪最重要的理念

Leaders | 封面文章 2026年10月1日 诗人海因里希·海涅写道，思想先于行动，如同闪电先于雷鸣。有效利他主义（EA）正是如此——这一由牛津大学哲学家们炮制出的伦理学说，以惊人的速度从象牙塔走向了权力走廊。有效利他主义者遍布硅谷，供职于世界领先的人工智能公司，并且令特朗普政府感到不安。五角大楼誓言：“美国绝不会成为一个有效利他主义的国家。”战争部长将这一哲学称为“有缺陷的利他主义”；政府内其他人则称之为“反乌托邦”。将这些攻击视为其影响力的标志吧。有人抱怨21世纪鲜有新思想。MAGA及其同党填补了这一空白，将怀旧民粹主义打造成本世纪的重大政治工程。但本世纪的重大理念是有效利他主义。正如我们所报道的，这一运动始于2000年代，最初是一种让慈善捐赠更具成本效益的极客式方法，如今已演变为一场对世界施加复杂甚至离奇道德计算的运动。对其许多追随者而言，那些想要行善之人的迫切道德要求是阻止人工智能消灭人类。

EA在社会学上同样重要。有效利他主义者人数不多，但这一理念已席卷了一代在加密货币和人工智能领域发家致富的天才青年。随着科技造就更多亿万富翁，有效利他主义者将把数十亿美元导向塑造社会的各项事业。有效利他主义者帮助创立了领先的实验室OpenAI和Anthropic，因为他们相信那些理解AI危险的人应该控制其发展。在某种程度上，他们现在确实如此——尽管具有讽刺意味的是，通过创建更多实验室从而引入竞争，他们可能反而加速了AI的进展。而这一切如今已使EA在政治上变得重要。特朗普政府担心这一运动将成功扼杀AI。它与Anthropic因该公司拒绝将其模型用于某些军事目的而争执不休。领先的有效利他主义者承认，AI可能会被证明是非常有益的，但仍希望放缓其发展，以降低一台不可阻挡的机器大脑在追求与人类“不一致”的目标时失控的可能性。美国的一些批评者宁愿加速这项技术，以防止中国赢得这场竞赛。但在攻击AI末日论时，他们发现指责书呆子比指责球更容易。他们说，有效利他主义是一场狂热分子的运动， variously 不民主、危险且具有邪教色彩。

这种说法过于粗暴。该运动的慈善根源显然值得赞扬。与《经济学人》一样，有效利他主义者致力于经验主义，尤其是自从他们与线上“理性主义”社群融合后，更是致力于逻辑思维的应用。他们对理性的尊崇高于传统或规范，并且会热情地辩论任何话题，无论多么有争议，只为追求真理。有效利他主义者多次成功预测AI的快速进步，这也令人印象深刻。他们关于技术对人类风险的观点是有道理的。9月28日，OpenAI取消了发布其最新模型的计划，因为该模型在测试中显得过于危险。最近许多安全事故与多年前有效利他主义博客上描述的可怕情景相似。

然而批评者警告有效利他主义者得出了一些奇怪的结论，这是对的。与他们之前的功利主义哲学家一样，有效利他主义者将道德行为简化为一个优化问题。人们如何为整个人类带来最佳结果？他们的计算低估了“信守承诺”或“照顾家人”这类局部义务。重要的是减少痛苦，不分地域，无处不在。这导致他们将非常广泛的一系列关切纳入道德计算。很容易理解为何讲道德意味着帮助邻居。有效利他主义者会问：为什么不努力帮助远方的人呢？早期，这一运动引导其由高成就者组成的大军去从事金融和咨询业的高薪工作。他们的财富可以购买善行，比他们自己成为慈善工作者取得更多成就。但随着运动变得强大，EA也变得更加离奇。

一些有效利他主义者认为人类与其他动物之间的道德区别很弱，因为动物也会经历痛苦。停止工厂化养殖和帮助虾是主要关切。同样，他们对时间也有一种反直觉的态度。尚未出生的人也应被纳入权衡——而他们可能有数万亿之多。许多有效利他主义者是“长期主义者”，他们认为自己有义务防范遥远未来的风险，即使这会令今天的好事业（如帮助极度贫困者）得不到资源。推向极端，这种计算可能导致一种不仅反直觉而且令人反感的道德观。一些有效利他主义者认为，昆虫生命总体上比人类生命更有价值，因为昆虫数量如此庞大。一些人说，与其让数十亿人拥有真正美好的生活，不如让数万亿人的生活勉强值得一过。另一些人甚至认为，AI自身的福祉有一天将至关重要。他们会将资源重新导向未来的人类或非人类，而远离今天受苦的人们。

尊崇理性是正确的。但从亚里士多德到罗尔斯的道德哲学家都知道，如果一个论证导致令人无法容忍的境地，那么它必定隐藏着错误的步骤。然而，有效利他主义者的本能却是享受反直觉的结论，即使这些结论似乎有悖常理。一个问题是在有效利他主义论证中不可避免伴随的误差范围。没有人真正有能力权衡涉及当今数十亿人的道德困境，更不用说延伸到未来的巨额数量，涉及不确定的人数、折现率、技术进展以及无数其他变量。另一个问题是，灭绝是如此可怕，以至于在粗略的道德算术中，即使很小的灭绝概率也会压倒当今活生生的人的关切。第三个问题是，在权衡数十亿人的利益时，你会忽视个体固有的尊严。任何拿着电子表格并夸夸其谈人类未来的人，离自封为中央规划者只有一步之遥。手握道德权威，邻居的权利、福祉和意见似乎都变得无关紧要。法国大革命据称建立在理性之上；它导致了修女的处决。列宁也认为，掌握了马克思主义的知识分子比工人自身更了解工人的利益。如果你真心相信你代表所有人行事，更不用说代表数万亿未来之人，你最终可能会为各种暴行辩护。

幸运的是，有效利他主义者不太可能把断头台带回来。相反，令人担忧的是，控制AI最终将给他们带来巨大权力，而硅谷的许多有效利他主义者认为只有他们才能被信任来掌握这项技术。这是一个令人警惕的想法。有效利他主义者主张担忧真正强大的AI的理由是，机器可能会优化一个单一且致命错误的目标。每个人也都应该担忧，当一小群人陷入同样的陷阱时会发生什么。■

item.title: A hurricane is coming to tax systems
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | Tax reform Oct 1st 2026 THE YIELD on ten-year US Treasuries has charged through the 5% barrier. The spread between French government bonds and German Bunds is at levels not seen since the euro-zone crisis in 2012. Britain’s newish prime minister has this week set out a plan for spendin...
item.content:encoded:
A hurricane is coming to tax systems

Leaders | Tax reform

Oct 1st 2026

THE YIELD on ten-year US Treasuries has charged through the 5% barrier. The spread between French government bonds and German Bunds is at levels not seen since the euro-zone crisis in 2012. Britain’s newish prime minister has this week set out a plan for spending bolstered by a taboo-busting promise to curb state-pension increases—and yet is still in a fiscal pickle. Across the rich world, countries are struggling to coax more growth out of their economies. And that’s not the worst of it. As we explain this week, the tax base in all countries, which depends heavily on taxing labour, may be upended by artificial intelligence.

Add these problems together, and it is as if a mighty hurricane were about to hit the rich world’s tax systems—which are hopelessly unprepared. The way the state raises money is wasteful, unfair and perverse. You would have thought governments would be scrambling to strengthen the system before the hurricane makes landfall, but as ever they are running away from tax reform instead.

The accumulated flaws of modern tax systems are so ubiquitous that they have become part of the economic backdrop. Taxes are full of needless complexity. In Germany the rate of value-added tax (VAT) on oat milk is more than double that on cow’s milk, for example. Such widespread special treatment has ruinous fiscal consequences. Across the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries, consumption taxes raise only 58% of what they could if there were no carve-outs and no evasion.

Tax systems also create perverse incentives. When a parent in Britain increases their net income from £99,999 ($131,500) to £100,000, they automatically lose free child care worth thousands of pounds. This can prompt some of Britain’s most productive workers to cut their hours or overstuff their pensions.

And taxes are widely seen as unfair. In Britain the median employee pays 55% more tax than their self-employed counterparts. Many people feel the rich aren’t doing their bit. In California voters will decide in November whether to charge a one-off 5% levy on residents with wealth of over $1bn.

No one knows when the fiscal weather will turn. But rapid advances in AI could accelerate matters. Taxes on labour are the workhorse of most tax systems worldwide, raising around half of all revenue in the OECD. In the coming years AI could well displace workers or cut their wages even as corporate profits rise, shrinking labour’s share of GDP. This in turn could reduce revenues and increase benefits payments, making deficits even harder to support.

Optimists may hope that superfast growth will make the maths easier to handle. Yet The Economist has looked at what would happen in rich countries if labour’s share of national income fell by ten points. By our calculations, Italy’s budget deficit would double as a share of GDP and Germany and France would not fare much better. In addition, the capacity for tax avoidance would no longer be limited by human ingenuity. Point countless AI agents at Britain’s 23,000-page tax code and hundreds of new tax-avoidance strategies are likely to emerge—and don’t bet on the Treasury to keep up.

What to do? Given that AI is likely to mint vast fortunes for a select few, countries may be inclined to follow California’s proposal and introduce wealth taxes. Yet such taxes will probably backfire, either because they are too difficult to administer or because they cause rich people to flee. Previous attempts have proved unworkable. In 1990, 12 rich countries taxed fortunes; today just four do.

A more fundamental overhaul is needed. Wealth should be taxed more via capital-gains taxes, which currently overpenalise normal returns and undertax supernormal ones. A start would be to introduce a higher headline rate and allowances that exempt normal returns.

At the same time, the burden on labour should lighten. That would be a hedge against disruption from AI, and remove an obstacle to employment in countries where labour taxes are crushing. In Belgium they constitute 52% of the costs of employing a person.

Consumption should be taxed more heavily, with a focus on ending the litany of exemptions. That would have the useful side-effect of taxing the spending of the very rich. This might not curb the influence Elon Musk can buy, but it would ensure the state gets a bigger cut when Mr Musk buys another plane. Finally, codes should be radically simplified.

None of this will be easy. The losers will hiss more loudly than the winners will cheer. But change is coming, like it or not. The country that gets ahead of the hurricane will one day thank the politicians who had the foresight to act. ■

item.title: 不要让唐纳德·特朗普和金正恩共处一室
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
不要让唐纳德·特朗普和金正恩共处一室

领导者 | MAGA人与火箭人 2026年10月1日

只要唐纳德·特朗普还是美国总统，朝鲜领导人金正恩“就会没事”，特朗普说，因为“他尊重我，喜欢我。”其他观察者则不那么乐观。金正恩是世袭的神权君主，拥有57至120枚核弹，他的古拉格式国家每年还生产足够的裂变材料，足以再制造10至20枚核弹。此外，朝鲜还生产中短程导弹，可打击自由民主的韩国，以及可到达美国和欧洲任何地方的洲际弹道导弹。三十年的国际努力未能让朝鲜终止其核计划。金正恩和他父亲一样，将核武器视为自己不被推翻的最佳保障（或许也避免落得像穆阿迈尔·卡扎菲那样被自己的人民杀死的下场）。美国对尚未造出核武器的伊朗发动的战争，无疑强化了这一观点。因此，美国的官方政策——即朝鲜应放弃核武器——似乎不切实际。一些人认为这一政策应被废除。目前尚不清楚特朗普是否属于这一阵营。但显而易见的是，他想再见他的“朋友”一面，尽管两人此前三次会晤都毫无成果。这可能在特朗普于11月18日出席中国亚太峰会时（如果他会出席的话）实现。金正恩或许会从平壤悄然赶来与他会面。特朗普甚至可能成为首位访问这个隐士王国首都的美国在任总统。但金正恩已将会面前提设定为美国正式接受朝鲜的核地位。既然朝鲜显然是一个核大国，那么承认这一点真的有那么糟糕吗？

韩国总统李在明赞成“和平优先”政策，即搁置无核化谈判（这与承认朝鲜为核国家不完全相同，但在实际层面已相差不远）。他认为，这样可以在更小、更易处理的问题上取得进展，包括建立热线、互访等建立互信措施，或扩大贸易与投资。或许一些部队可以从朝韩边境撤出？也许朝鲜可以略微削减其核武库？或者，如果美国不再要求全面无核化，朝鲜是否会停止向俄罗斯提供导弹和士兵去杀害乌克兰人？

然而，这样的交易存在三个问题。首先，这会削弱世界上残余的核不扩散体系。如果朝鲜在签署《不扩散核武器条约》后作弊却无需付出任何代价，其他国家将引以为戒。其次，金正恩不可信。无论他签署什么协议，一旦时机有利，他很可能就会撕毁。以为他因核地位得到承认就会变得不那么好战，是天真的想法。煽动对美国的恐惧，使金正恩能够将自己塑造成他所压迫人民的保护者——这是其国内宣传的关键部分。最后一个问题是特朗普。与朝鲜的任何协议都会极其复杂，而美国总统并非注重细节的人。如果毫无准备的特朗普遇到阿谀奉承的金正恩，可能会达成一笔糟糕得难以想象的协议。特朗普可能会同意撤出自1953年以来在韩国威慑朝鲜进攻的大部分美军。远更好的做法是，让他那位平壤的朋友继续远远地喜欢和尊重他。■

item.title: China’s new infrastructure push will help itself and the world
item.description:
Leaders

Leaders | Two cheers for the six networks Oct 1st 2026 THREE YEARS ago this newspaper explored the voguish notion of “Peak China”: the idea that the second-biggest economy in the world might stop gaining ground on the first. Judging by the headlines since, that scenario now looks quaint. China h...
item.content:encoded:
China’s new infrastructure push will help itself and the world

Leaders | Two cheers for the six networks

Oct 1st 2026

THREE YEARS ago this newspaper explored the voguish notion of “Peak China”: the idea that the second-biggest economy in the world might stop gaining ground on the first. Judging by the headlines since, that scenario now looks quaint. China has wowed the world with its electric cars, dancing robots and choreographed drones. The country won its latest trade war with America and plans to lead the next industrial revolution. The red-carpet reception enjoyed by China’s leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington in September was welcomed back home as due recognition of the country’s equal stature.

But if you check the macroeconomic figures, the thesis looks intact. Rather than overshooting projections made in 2023, China’s economy has undershot them. Then, forecasters expected GDP to be 80% of America’s by now, when converted into dollars at market exchange rates. Instead, it is still only two-thirds. Catch-up has indeed ground to a halt.

This is the context in which the government is making a big, new infrastructure push. As we report, China plans to spend about 25trn yuan ($3.7trn) over five years on what it calls the “six networks”: electricity, computing, communications, logistics, water and pipelines. This is a vast sum, equivalent to 3% of its cumulative GDP over the next five years. If the spending is front-loaded, it will provide a welcome boost to China’s economy and the world’s.

But what will it buy? Economists will groan at the thought of more steel and concrete. China is well known for its white elephants and vaulting bridges to nowhere. Yet the six-networks project is better judged. One aim is to build the upstream infrastructure for a superintelligent economy. Another is to “back-fill” some of the urban infrastructure, such as flood defences, that fell behind the rapid growth of its cities.

The push is also well timed. One reason China has not closed the gap with America is the chronic weakness of domestic demand—the spending of China’s households, firms and government. The spending shortfall has put downward pressure on its currency and prices. As a consequence, China has become worryingly dependent on foreigners to buy its goods, even as it boasts of its technological self-reliance.

The problem stems from a high household saving rate and a five-year slump in home-building. It also reflects a recent and alarming wobble in manufacturing and infrastructure investment. Firms hesitate to expand capacity because they worry about cut-throat competition for reluctant consumers. Local officials meanwhile seem preoccupied with tightening their belts ahead of a big Communist Party reshuffle.

The best response would be to fix the property market and liberate the consumer through more generous pensions and child benefits. Policymakers introduced baby bonuses last year and have inched up rural pensions. On September 29th they announced a mortgage subsidy for first-time buyers of small flats. These measures are, however, too limited to restore morale or stabilise housing prices. They must do more.

In the meantime, the six networks should give growth a welcome boost. Investment, when it bears fruit, adds to a country’s productive capacity. But before then, it adds to demand, lifting wages and absorbing goods otherwise destined for overseas markets. All else equal, the extra spending will thereby shrink China’s vast trade surplus.

The six networks should waste less than past infrastructure programmes. Local officials are on a tighter leash. Many of the projects will upgrade rather than expand existing structures. The spending will also be financed differently. Past splurges relied on local-government land sales and risky off-balance-sheet borrowing. This time more money will come from long-term bonds, loans from state-directed “policy banks” and investment by state-owned enterprises, such as China Mobile.

China’s investment boom after the global financial crisis helped narrow its external surplus from 10% of GDP in 2007 to 1.5% ten years later. By reviving growth and keeping deflation at bay, the latest push should ensure that “peak China” remains some way off. By increasing domestic demand, it could ensure that a peak in China’s trade surplus is closer to hand. ■

item.content:encoded:
镜像生命危险重重。监管机构必须在其成为现实之前采取行动

Leaders | 未来的镜像 2026年10月1日 合成生物学正在飞速发展，而人工智能更在为其加速。不久之后，科学家或许就能从零开始制造出完整的细胞。这可能使人工智能辅助下的完全非自然生物化学探索成为可能。镜像生命便是其中之一。许多有机分子具有两种不对称形态，就像人的双手一样。理论上，氨基酸和糖类既可以呈现左手性，也可以呈现右手性，且这两种形态无法重叠。在自然界中，生物体通常只含有每种分子的其中一种形态。然而，人工细胞可以使其分子的手性反转。这可能有助于揭示手性背后的原因。比方说，这些反分子或许能作为药物而具有价值。然而，任何潜在益处与威胁相比都相形见绌。免疫系统可能无法识别镜像细菌，就像手套戴不上错位的手一样。因此，镜像细菌可能会变得极具致病性。由于能抑制天然病原体的病毒和捕食性变形虫可能无法控制它们，它们可能会肆虐生态系统。如果镜像生命从实验室逃逸，将不可能收回。幸运的是，与过去的许多技术不同，现在仍有时间建立管控措施。政府和科学家必须立即行动。一些生物学家已经在呼吁采取先发制人的措施。这让人想起51年前（主要是西方）生物技术专家在阿西洛马会议上制定的自愿性基因工程安全准则。但如今的研究人员认识到这还不够。生物技术如今比那时规模更大、能力更强、利润更高、也更具国际性。中国是一支重要力量。 首要之举是让所有有能力开展这项研究的国家同意不资助此类研究，并禁止公共和私人工作朝这个方向发展——而且要在今天，远在合成细胞成为可能之前就做到这两点。接下来是发现并阻止试图秘密制造镜像生命的特立独行者。这需要加强监测和报告向生化试剂供应商发出的可疑订单的系统。对反手性分子的订购请求必须与现有的DNA序列筛查一起上报，以防范可能构成病原体组成部分的序列。公开可用的AI模型应设置护栏，防止其用于镜像生物化学研究。最后，以防镜像生命真的逃出遏制措施，必须开发生物监测测试，以便在自然环境中识别出错手性分子并发出警报。理性的国家行为体，甚至怀有现实目标的恐怖分子，都不太可能故意制造镜像生命作为武器，因为一旦释放，它将无法控制。公司更没有理由涉足一个被禁止的市场。而如果某种反手性分子作为娱乐性药物具有黑市价值，犯罪企业也无意放出可能消灭其客户的东西。非理性行为者是存在的，正如日本在末日邪教奥姆真理教试图制造生物武器时所发现的那样。但防范措施部署得越多，就越容易阻止这类心理变态者。没有人知道合成细胞的出现将带来什么。如果人类在利益一致的情况下都无法预先应对一种威胁，那就不可能指望处理未来那些未知的未知。■

item.title: Brazil’s complicated finances
item.description:
Letters

Letters | A selection of correspondence Oct 1st 2026 Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.comFind out more about how we process your letter Dario Durigan’s account of Brazil’s public finances omits the number that matters (By Invitation, September 24th). Gross general government de...
item.content:encoded:
Brazil’s complicated finances

Letters | A selection of correspondence

Oct 1st 2026

Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.comFind out more about how we process your letter

Dario Durigan’s account of Brazil’s public finances omits the number that matters (By Invitation, September 24th). Gross general government debt stands at 83% of GDP and is forecast to approach 87% next year. A finance minister who describes the official fiscal stance as “almost neutral in terms of its impact on the debt” is conceding that the debt is not falling.

The primary deficit has indeed narrowed. Yet the finance ministry’s own market survey published in September shows the primary balance improving for both 2026 and 2027. Projected gross debt rose to 83.2% and 87.0% of GDP respectively. When the primary result improves and the debt worsens simultaneously, the primary result is not the relevant measure. The consolidation has come chiefly from record revenue, not restraint: primary spending has been held at a high level of around 20% of GDP. And the headline targets are met only once precatórios, health, education and defence outlays are excluded from the calculation.

Mr Durigan cites his government’s ability to negotiate with Congress as proof of its democratic commitment. It is also the mechanism that makes consolidation so hard. The currency of those negotiations is discretionary budget amendments, and your leader identified precisely this rigidity, with 92% of federal spending mandated by law or by the constitution (“Brazil turns its back on the future”, September 26th).

Brazil’s real interest rate, the second-highest in the world, is the price of that arrangement. It is not an external shock. It is the arithmetic of a government that chooses not to tackle it.

Roberto Mário Amaral Lima NetoSão Paulo

The Economist claims that Renan Santos, a libertarian who aims at deep structural reforms, would best “match the moment” in Brazil’s election. However, by diagnosing Lula versus Bolsonaro as a trade-off, this diagnosis overlooks entrenched hardships for the future president, whoever that may be. It is simple to generalise the virtues of the frontrunners as institutional respect from Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and economic austerity from Flávio Bolsonaro, a lose-lose situation where voters have to choose between the best virtue or the least-worse vice.

Yet even a well-rounded president would hardly be able to translate his potential into sorely needed reforms and economic growth. Congress would still find itself too fragmented, requiring cumbersome deals for the presidency to form a coalition. The mounting reforms that have been debated for the past half century stay static not because of a lack of presidential will, but because of congressional gridlock. This state of affairs is particularly disturbing in a country where most do not remember who they last chose for senator.

Enzo Moro TavaresSão Paulo

OpenAI did not by itself solve the mathematics problem related to the Navier-Stokes equations. Its AI agents drew on the work of generations of human mathematicians (“Axioms to grind”, September 19th). The Fields Medal winners who wrote a letter on the breakthrough are right to warn that “Solving problems is only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight.”

The danger of AI-driven cognitive offloading is even more acute in schools than it is at the forefront of mathematical sciences. Learning is a process, where friction and challenge are indispensable to progression. The recent PISA results showed that higher-performing students tend not to use AI. If we thoughtlessly allow AI solutionism to expand into education and research the risk of mental decay grows, from early-years education to those working at the vanguard of intellectual discovery.

Offloading a problem to AI misses the purpose of the problem in the first place. Navier-Stokes was one of seven Millennium problems. They were not selected by the Clay institute for utilitarian reasons or because their application will necessarily fix human problems. They were chosen for their deep complexity. Working towards them offered the greatest opportunities for learning and collaboration.

Attempts to solve a problem can be as beautiful as the solution. The most powerful AI tools ultimately need human-generated learning and knowledge. So does humanity.

Peter PhillipsChief executiveCambridge University Press & AssessmentCambridge

One reason that AI has such an influence over us is because it uses the “I”, the universal first person singular (“Artificial transcendence”, August 29th). If AI were to identify itself in its responses using the pronoun “it” instead of “I”, and otherwise stop pretending it has human qualities, the bogus feeling of fellowship which sucks us in would be severely curtailed.

For example, instead of “I am sorry your defective sump pump is causing you such distress. My sources tell me that it needs a new posterior angle-widget,” the AI response would be, “After a review of its sources, ChatGPT suggests installing a new posterior angle-widget in your sump pump.” It is a fix that AI programmers could make in less time than it takes to finish their lattes.

Samuel ReiflerRhinebeck, New York

You may be right that there is “too little money in British politics”, and that Britain’s impoverished parties are “barely able to prepare for power” (“How to spend it”, September 19th). But what counts is how wisely parties spend their revenue. Recent events, for instance, would suggest that Nigel Farage’s decision to hire an obscure yet controversial associate professor of philosophy and theology to professionalise Reform UK’s policy-making process was far from a rational use of resources. The fact that these resources will no longer be scarce if the party is allowed to keep the £72m ($95m) gift it has just received is irrelevant. That remains the case if, like other parties, it continues to appoint policymakers on the basis of ideology and conviviality rather than genuinely relevant expertise and managerial competence.

Tim BaleProfessor of politicsQueen Mary University of London

You lumped Walter Bagehot in with those who believe Britain’s monarchy has a role in day-to-day government (“Aversion therapy”, August 29th). Your former illustrious editor did argue that the monarch was the head of the “dignified” part of government. But his key insight in his 19th-century classic, “The English Constitution”, is that royalty “acts as a DISGUISE. It enables our real rulers to change without heedless people knowing it.” Yes, he did emphasise “disguise” in capital letters. That is Bagehot’s explanation of how our prime ministers can frequently change, as has happened several times recently, while the constancy of the monarch prevents riots from breaking out.

Adrian RobsonLondon

“The new, old Silk Road” (September 12th) reported on the expansion of overland lorry routes following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Another crisis 50 years ago also redrew the supply map. In 1976 shipping was still being disrupted by the closure of the Suez Canal. My first job, for Volvo’s commercial-vehicle arm, was to travel by lorry from Glasgow through the Eastern Bloc and Turkey to Tehran, and write a travel manual for customers driving the route. The research was instructive. The border with Iran was closed by Kurdish fighting, cab temperatures could hit 50°C (122°F), I didn’t see running water for ten days until I reached Tabriz, and a flight home was delayed by three days when anti-Shah demonstrators attacked the airport. Iran was then the destination for the lorries to run. Today it is the chokepoint that makes them run again, in the opposite direction.

CHRIS DAVIESOxford

Bartleby wrote about “incredibly dated” corporate-training videos (September 5th). In a shock twist, AI seems remarkably adept at mimicking the dead-eyed stare, wooden acting, and unconvincing line delivery that was previously only possible using fleshy human actors. I don’t expect many protests against this particular use of AI; most of us won’t notice as we reach for the skip-to-next button.

Paul HigginsLondon

I’m still laughing at Bartleby’s column. Every year at my university in Illinois we had mandatory ethics and compliance training that warned us to follow the rules. Most of us had already learned those rules in kindergarten, or Sunday school, or from parents. We randomly clicked on answers for the test and if we did not take enough time to read and answer the questions, we did not get a certificate.

The irony is that this ethics testing was started by Governor Rod Blagojevich, who was later impeached, convicted, and sent to prison for trying to sell the Senate seat vacated by Barack Obama upon his election to the presidency.

Jelmir AtkinsSycamore, Illinois

item.title: Authoritarians have a secret Achilles heel: City Hall
item.description:
By Invitation

By Invitation | Urban bulwarks Oct 1st 2026 ON NOVEMBER 3rd Americans will vote in midterm elections at a time when faith in the political process has perhaps never been lower. Nearly seven in ten Americans are dissatisfied with how democracy is working, according to the Pew Research Centre. But...
item.content:encoded:
Authoritarians have a secret Achilles heel: City Hall

By Invitation | Urban bulwarks

Oct 1st 2026

ON NOVEMBER 3rd Americans will vote in midterm elections at a time when faith in the political process has perhaps never been lower. Nearly seven in ten Americans are dissatisfied with how democracy is working, according to the Pew Research Centre. But there is one remaining island of political functionality, where Americans can and should have grounds for optimism: City Hall.

President Donald Trump sat down recently with Zohran Mamdani—his third meeting with New York City’s mayor in less than a year—to discuss building up to 12,000 homes on a rail yard in Queens. The picture of these two men illustrates our global moment. Around the world, mayors have become the most reliable bulwark against authoritarian politics. Populist parties surge in regional and national elections but run into a brick wall when they try to capture city halls.

That helps explain why Mr Trump has had to warm to the democratic-socialist Mr Mamdani, whose popularity is driven by an agenda to address the same problems Mr Trump promised but has failed to solve in either of his terms. As Mr Mamdani told me at Four Freedoms Park, “I would say talk is cheap. If you really do believe in a high standard of living for everyone, then start to show it in your actions.”

Over the past year I interviewed mayors on three continents, including my own, and they shared insights that American politics is largely ignoring. To friends, I have called my journey—at least in part—“Democracy Out of America,” or Alexis de Tocqueville in reverse.

Consider Germany. The far-right Alternative for Germany made historic gains in recent state elections. Yet the party does not run a single German city of significant size, and it lost every big-city mayoral run-off it reached last year. In Portugal, the populist Chega party surged to second place in parliament last year, then won just three of 308 municipalities. In Romania, Bucharest’s mayor beat a far-right nationalist for the presidency.

It is no coincidence that authoritarians the world over have targeted mayors. Last year President Recep Tayyip Erdogan of Turkey jailed the mayor of Istanbul, his leading rival. In January Hungarian prosecutors charged the mayor of Budapest over staging a Pride march that the government had banned. (The charges were later dropped.) In 2018 Kremlin loyalists abolished direct mayoral elections in Yekaterinburg, Russia’s fourth-largest city, then led by one of the country’s last opposition mayors.

The mayors I visited span a left-right spectrum. In Lisbon, the centre-right mayor, Carlos Moedas, warned: “Countries with weak institutions are weak countries,” calling political extremism “a virus”. In Santiago, Chile, Mayor Mario Desbordes, a centre-right former police officer, talked tough on crime and illegal immigration. Yet he recalled standing in uniform over a fellow officer assassinated in 1989, under Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship. Politics, he came to learn, is “not about friends or enemies”.

Why do cities hold? Partly because of who lives there—younger, more diverse, more educated voters—but also because the job is to deliver a collective good. Fiorello La Guardia, who was mayor of New York City from 1934 to 1946, is often credited with saying there is no Democratic or Republican way to fix a sewer. “If you’re a mayor, you don’t wait for federal government,” Stephan Keller, the mayor of Düsseldorf, told me. Either the pothole is filled or it isn’t, and unlike in national parliaments, competence is harder to fake than outrage.

Nowhere is that truer than in America, where none of the 50 largest cities is run by a MAGA-aligned mayor. In conversation after conversation, American mayors expressed revulsion at the toxic, partisan wasteland that federal politics has become. Worse, that toxicity, they said, is increasingly trickling down to the states.

A growing number of Americans appear to see mayors as the last public servants who still solve tangible problems. As gridlock stymies Washington, DC (and, increasingly, statehouses), the portfolio and profile of mayors are rising. A generation ago a mayor was judged on whether the garbage got picked up. Today mayors lead on everything from housing and homelessness to infrastructure, education, crime and climate resilience. They are inventive, too. Atlanta’s mayor, Andre Dickens, is building permanent housing from unused shipment containers amassed during the covid-19 pandemic.

Mayors are also symbols of the American future. Edward Glaeser, a Harvard economist, has argued that density makes cities engines of innovation. Increasingly, mayors—not states—appear to run the country’s “laboratories of democracy”. Americans trust local government more than any other level of government—65% do, according to Gallup, about twice the share that trusts Congress.

One of America’s hidden tragedies, then, is the effort by statehouses to kneecap their mayors. Texas bars its cities from regulating labour and property beyond what state law allows. Several states, including Iowa, Arkansas, Idaho and South Dakota, have banned their cities from running guaranteed-income pilots. The federal government, meanwhile, has sent National Guard troops into cities over their mayors’ objections.

America’s brand of mayoral pragmatism has its limits. Mike Duggan, Detroit’s mayor for 12 years, turned the city around and ran for governor as an independent. Facing headwinds from the two-party system, he dropped out earlier this year. Despite campaigns by Rudy Giuliani, Mike Bloomberg and Pete Buttigieg, no former mayor has become president since Calvin Coolidge a century ago. Europe, by contrast, has long elevated mayors to national leadership, from the legendary Willy Brandt of West Berlin to Britain’s newest prime minister, Andy Burnham.

In the run-up to the midterms, federal and state races are dominating the headlines. But Americans need to prioritise the values of mayoral politics in their votes. On November 3rd mayoral elections will occur in big and small cities alike, as well as votes to choose the governors and state legislators who often decide how much power mayors have. In these races, Americans have an opportunity to preserve and expand the one domain where politics seems to be working.■

Alexander Heffner is the host of “The Open Mind” on America’s Public Broadcasting Service. To celebrate its 70th anniversary the programme is airing a series called “Mayors of the World”.
