item.content:encoded:
伊朗是否已失去对海湾石油出口的控制？

中东与非洲 | 回归矿山 2026年10月1日 9月26日，唐纳德·特朗普拒绝了伊朗提出的 ceasefire 提议，该提议本会在七天内重新开放霍尔木兹海峡。总统表示，伊朗想要达成协议是因为它“输得太惨了”。特朗普及其许多顾问认为，美国等待更久会获得更多好处。 海湾地区流出的石油量似乎证明他是对的。船舶追踪公司Kpler估计，迄今为止，该地区阿拉伯国家在9月份平均每日运送1700万桶原油和成品油，前提是包括通过霍尔木兹海峡以及通过管道绕行该海峡的流量。这是自2月以来的最高水平，接近战前每日2100万桶的总量（见图表1）。相比之下，伊朗仅出口每日20万桶，不到冲突开始前运量的十分之一。从7000英里外的华盛顿来看，伊朗对海湾石油的扼制似乎正在松动。但真是如此吗？全球基准布伦特原油仍停留在每桶100美元左右——比6月美国与伊朗达成（临时）协议时高出约40%，尽管当时的出口量还低四分之一。问题不在于令人瞠目的运费：油轮租赁费率处于创纪录水平，但布伦特期货报价为“船上交货”，反映的是装货时而非交货时的原油价格。相反，三个原因突出：原油供应仍落后于需求；美国柴油出口禁令的前景正在扭曲市场；以及人们日益担心伊朗可能再次袭击船只或能源基础设施。先看供需失衡。通过霍尔木兹海峡的流量激增，是因为沙特阿拉伯正通过该通道输送比战争初期多得多的石油。9月28日，沙特阿美邀请中国炼油商对下月装载的原油进行竞标，此前两周已通过两轮销售售出超过9000万桶。现在，沙特大部分石油在美国护航下，由国有油轮穿梭通过海峡，然后在阿曼湾转移到其他船只上。阿联酋也采用类似策略。国有船只比私人船只更能抵抗压力，因此即使伊朗再次发出好战言论，流量也未曾停止。但沙特官员自己承认，这种船对船转运方案成本高昂、笨拙且不可持续。海湾供应仍比战前水平低每日400万桶。在俄罗斯入侵乌克兰、布伦特原油触及129美元峰值后，世界曾担心可能面临类似的短缺。 与此同时，全球原油需求已经回升。中国在夏季将原油购买量削减近40%后，再次渴求石油（见图表2）。国内航空燃油、柴油和汽油库存下降如此之快，以至于批发燃料价格现已超过零售价格（零售价受政府限制）。因此，炼油厂正更加努力地满足国内市场。在中国于10月1日看似重新实施出口限制之前，它们也一直在增加进口以用于出口，因为全球燃料短缺预示着海外利润丰厚。最近几周，由于预期限制措施，进口以出口的采购量可能更高。中国还不得不替代其过去从伊朗购买的石油。这迫使其在公开市场上购买更多原油，推高了官方价格。与伊朗产油最相似的原油价格涨幅甚至超过布伦特：迪拜期货交易价为每桶116美元。但中国也在与欧洲买家竞争类似北海的原油品种，同时也推高了布伦特价格。 结果是，全球原油供应仍低于需求。追踪未来几周装船石油的即期布伦特价格徘徊在每桶120美元左右（见图表3）。它通常与布伦特期货相差几美元；异常大的价差表明现货市场吃紧。布伦特价格也受到另一个市场——柴油——短缺的推动。海湾流量有限以及俄罗斯的出口禁令已使主要市场的柴油批发价格推高至近200美元。美国油价仍接近每加仑6.50美元的创纪录水平，在中期选举前几周激怒了卡车司机和农民。特朗普表示，他赞成限制这种燃料的出口，自战争开始以来，大量柴油已流向欧洲。这将削减对美国原油的需求，因为那里的炼油厂将加工更少的原油，同时欧洲炼油商试图生产更多柴油也会提升对其他等级原油的需求。这一前景已使布伦特价格比美国基准西德克萨斯中质原油高出12美元。这就留下了第三个风险：伊朗可能再次发起攻击。其强硬派统治者必然对霍尔木兹海峡交通摆脱其控制感到愤恨。9月30日报告了三起针对油轮的袭击，但自9月23日以来，伊朗未使任何一艘油轮瘫痪。但这种情况可能改变。未经证实的报告表明，伊朗已在海峡布设新水雷，或正准备布设。航运情报公司Windward于9月26日探测到75艘能够部署漂移弹药的高速艇在阿曼海岸附近蜂拥而出。伊朗仍有能力打击海湾油田和能源设施。沙特阿拉伯的东-西管道在9月初遭袭并部分修复，仍然脆弱。沙特港口也是如此。伊朗支持的也门胡塞叛军可能进一步限制曼德海峡（一条重要的红海航运路线）的交通。出口增加并不意味着霍尔木兹海峡变得更安全；它们仅表明石油工业已适应在持续风险下运营。这种风险仍可能成为现实并再次扼杀流量。过去的霍尔木兹表现不能保证未来结果——尤其是当伊朗感到走投无路时。■ 更正（10月1日）：本文早期版本称伊朗提出开放霍尔木兹海峡七天。实际是提出在七天内开放。抱歉。

item.title: Jared Kushner has a $2.45bn recovery plan for Gaza
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | Inhabiting the uninhabitable Oct 1st 2026 A year ago Donald Trump set up his Board of Peace (bop), a private club of world leaders. The day that he announced his plan for redevelopment in Gaza, to be overseen by the board, was, he claimed, “potentially one of the great...
item.content:encoded:
Jared Kushner has a $2.45bn recovery plan for Gaza

Middle East & Africa | Inhabiting the uninhabitable

Oct 1st 2026

A year ago Donald Trump set up his Board of Peace (bop), a private club of world leaders. The day that he announced his plan for redevelopment in Gaza, to be overseen by the board, was, he claimed, “potentially one of the greatest days ever in civilisation”. The outfit has spent a year carrying out “intense preparation”, according to Tony Blair, a former British prime minister and member of the board’s executive. Now comes “the implementation”.

On September 23rd on the sidelines of the un General Assembly Jared Kushner, Mr Trump’s son-in-law and one of his main fixers, gave a sense of what the board hopes to spend on that implementation. He announced a $2.45bn recovery plan and talked of $71bn for a decade of reconstruction. The board would oversee 66 projects over the next six months alone, he declared. Power-point presentations promised a “connected, prosperous Gaza delivering Security, Dignity and Opportunity”.

Such promises ring hollow in Gaza. Israel has depopulated the nearly two-thirds of Gaza it occupies. Military outposts dot the strip. Herds of bulldozers level the rubble, erasing property boundaries and evidence of what some have judged to be war crimes. The first contours are emerging of what America says will be “alternative safe communities” for vetted Palestinians. Safe communities, reply hardline Israeli ministers, for Jewish settlers.

Israel bombs tents and the few houses still standing almost daily. It says it is pursuing the remaining leaders of Hamas, the Islamist group that broke out of Gaza and massacred Israelis three years ago. Over 1,400 people have been killed in the year since the ceasefire. Forget building new shelters ahead of winter. Heavy machinery to clear 68m tonnes of debris and to repair schools, hospitals, electricity and sanitation is banned on grounds of “dual use”. Even tent poles are forbidden.

Hamas remains the de facto authority. From bombed-out buildings it is still registering births and collecting sales taxes. But its hold is strained. In September Israel killed commanders in four of Gaza’s five governorates. To avoid being spotted by Israeli troops, police wear plain clothes.

Some warn of a descent into al-falatan al-amni, the security chaos that preceded the collapse of the Palestinian Authority in Gaza in the mid-2000s. Palestinian militias, backed by Israel, prey on Hamas. As the group’s rule frays, clans have returned to the streets, brandishing their weapons. Squabbles about jumping queues for bread and water end in gun battles. Mugging, once a rarity, is rife. Unable to provide for Gaza’s mass of orphans, relatives sell children for marriage. Some wives are as young as 12, said a recent un report. One man, said researchers, had married off his young daughter for two sacks of flour. “Gazans have lost our kindness,” says a Hamas civil servant. “We’ve grown cruel.”

In a warehouse the board set up a year ago in Kiryat Gat, an Israeli city 20km from Gaza, military personnel, spooks, diplomats and aid workers co-ordinate Gaza’s reconstruction with Israel. But the “initial momentum has stagnated”, says a Western official who spent months there. For all Mr Kushner’s talk of billions, funding for the board’s projects has fallen far short as Gulf donors have prioritised needs at home.

But the real obstacle, say officials working in Kiryat Gat, is Israel. The number of aid agencies in Gaza has fallen. The troops offered by five countries for the International Stabilisation Force to monitor the truce and oversee Israel’s withdrawal have not been allowed to enter. The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the Palestinian body appointed by the board to replace Hamas, is stuck in Egypt, as are 450 vetted Palestinian police officers. The board’s biggest effort to tackle hunger has been the canteen providing free buffets to staff in Kiryat Gat, quip officials, at a cost of $9m in six months (the price of about 1,800 community kitchens in Gaza). “The bop is always pandering to the Israelis,” says a Western official who visits frequently.

Some hope for change after Israel’s election on October 27th. But even if he is defeated Mr Netanyahu may cling on for months as caretaker, as Israel’s fragmented political parties jostle over forming a governing coalition. Moreover, the result might be another lurch to the right. Calls for “voluntary migration” of Palestinians, an Israeli euphemism for expulsion, are growing. One candidate, Moshe Feiglin, has said that every baby in Gaza is an enemy. Even more centrist contenders for prime minister share Mr Netanyahu’s view that Hamas must still be crushed.

Israel remains determined to do this militarily. In August Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s “high representative” in Gaza, persuaded the Islamists to agree to hand over their weapons in exchange for an Israeli withdrawal. Much in his plan was unclear. Would Hamas disarm before, in tandem with or after an Israeli withdrawal? Would its Palestinian adversaries disarm? Would Hamas give up light weapons as well as heavy ones? But Hamas was spared hard choices. Mr Netanyahu rejected the plan and a troop withdrawal. “Even if Hamas fully disarms, Israel would still claim it has a penknife,” says a European official.

Others are still trying to drag Hamas onto a political path. Given a green light from Mr Kushner, who has met its leaders, Muhammad Dahlan, a former warlord from Gaza who fought Hamas, is leading talks with the group in Cairo. His negotiators say he has persuaded Hamas to accept terms set by Mahmoud Abbas, the Palestinian president, for taking part in Palestinian elections in November. “We’ve been successful in changing Hamas’s minds,” claims Osama al-Fara, a former mayor in Gaza and an ally of Mr Dahlan. These include, he says, recognising Israel and accepting previous Palestinian agreements with it. This time, however, the spoiler may not be Israel. Fearing defeat, Mr Abbas is expected to cancel the elections. ■

item.title: Nigerians dislike their president, but may re-elect him anyway
item.description:
Middle East & Africa

Middle East & Africa | Advantage Tinubu Oct 1st 2026 With just over three months to go until Nigerians vote for a president, the incumbent does not look particularly worried about his re-election prospects. On September 29th Bola Tinubu (pictured), who expects to win a second term in January...
item.content:encoded:
Nigerians dislike their president, but may re-elect him anyway

Middle East & Africa | Advantage Tinubu

Oct 1st 2026

With just over three months to go until Nigerians vote for a president, the incumbent does not look particularly worried about his re-election prospects. On September 29th Bola Tinubu (pictured), who expects to win a second term in January, returned from Paris after a month-long stay in Europe. He had previously extended his “working holiday” by several days, raising eyebrows at home.

On the face of it, Mr Tinubu’s cool is surprising. Nigeria is suffering a worsening security crisis, with people kidnapped and killed by bandits or insurgents on a near-daily basis. His economic reforms, though lauded by investors, have yet to make life better for most of the country’s 240m people. Add to that political challengers who are more popular than him, especially in the northern states worst affected by violence and economic deprivation, and the president should be quaking in his suede loafers. That he is not says less about him and more about Nigeria’s complicated electoral dynamics.

To understand the misery over which Mr Tinubu and his ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) have been presiding, consider Borno, in Nigeria’s north-east. The poor state, which the APC also runs, is in the grip of an insurgency that has raged unchecked for two decades. Jihadists fight both the government and each other. Rival factions make money by kidnapping schoolchildren and extorting or looting cash and grain from already poor farmers. Such violence has wrecked the economy, leaving young people jobless and traders without customers. One 27-year-old in Maiduguri, the capital, complains that he is forced to travel to neighbouring Chad to sell his grain, as locals cannot afford it. Youngsters “pack all their things and leave Borno state” for Chad, Cameroon or Ghana, he says, “because if you sit down here, there is no food in this country.”

Mr Tinubu’s re-election pitch is focused on reforms, such as the abolition of a pricey fuel subsidy, that have brought a degree of stability to Nigeria. Inflation has fallen, government revenue is rising and investment is picking up. But in Borno the reforms—combined with a lean harvest, aid cuts and rising energy prices following the wars in Ukraine and Iran—have made life harder. The annual inflation rate in August was still around 15%, with food inflation closer to 20%. Few people can afford enough to eat, prompting a hunger crisis in Borno and in neighbouring states (see map). The UN’s World Food Programme reckons malnutrition in the state is at its worst level for a decade.

Dr Nura Tukur, who runs a clinic for the starving operated by Save the Children, a charity, says there has been a sharp increase in the number of malnourished women and babies admitted over the past three years. July was the worst month since the clinic opened in 2016. Aisha Umara, who arrived several months ago with two starving triplets (one had died on the way), is now healthy enough to breastfeed. But her two six-month-olds still weigh just 2.5kg each. They are unlikely to survive being discharged to a home with no food in a village ruled by jihadists.

All this has hurt Mr Tinubu’s reputation in the north, where his party has traditionally done well, even though he personally lacks a base there. In the election in 2023 he won 54% of the vote in Borno. But recent polling by SBM Intelligence, a risk-advisory firm, suggests he is now less popular in the state than Peter Obi, another presidential candidate from the south, and Atiku Abubakar, a candidate with a big base in the north-east.

Some of Maiduguri’s residents say they are prepared to “fight back” at the ballot box in January. Yet in general, Mr Tinubu’s unpopularity will probably not be enough to dislodge him from the presidency. Incumbents, with access to the ruling-party machinery and plentiful cash to dole out goodies, have tended to have an advantage in recent Nigerian elections. It helps that the opposition is splintered and disorganised. Mr Obi has failed to form a coalition with Mr Abubakar. “Because it’s not a united ticket, that anti-APC vote is not coalesced into a single vote,” says Joachim MacEbong of Control Risks, a consultancy. In Maiduguri some people say they do not even know who else is on the ballot besides Mr Tinubu.

It also helps that Mr Tinubu and his vice-presidential candidate (who is a former governor of Borno state) are both Muslim, as are most people in the north. “The fact that the president has stuck with the Muslim-Muslim ticket resonates with quite a number of people,” says Cheta Nwanze, the boss of SBM Intelligence. Even voters who like Mr Obi may rule him out because he is a Catholic; the fact that he has a Muslim running-mate may not be enough.

Perhaps most significantly, voters in the north may not be too concerned by Mr Tinubu’s record because they already expect little from the government. “Many people are living where there has been no real security, no real health care, no real schools. Over time, people’s expectations get lower and lower,” says Mr MacEbong. One mother in Maiduguri says she will vote for Mr Tinubu as a “thank you” for the medicine at the government hospital. With their home state badly governed for so long, many people are more likely to trust God and their families to improve their lives than a government that rarely has.

Such cynicism is not limited to Borno. As long as the security crisis remains unresolved and economic growth, which is expected to hit 4.1% this year, does not translate into concrete improvements in Nigerians’ daily lives, many voters will remain disappointed. Yet few will use the ballot box to express their disappointment. In Borno, where a journey to the polling station could easily entail an encounter with militants, most will probably not bother voting at all. In 2023 turnout in the state was below 20%, even less than the dismal 27% nationwide. In parts of the south, especially Mr Tinubu’s home of Lagos, plenty may swallow whatever bad feelings they have about their day-to-day struggles and vote for their “son”. No wonder Mr Tinubu feels safe enough to take extended holidays in Paris. ■

item.title: How will AI philanthropy change development aid?
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
How will AI philanthropy change development aid?

Middle East & Africa | Artificial altruism

Oct 1st 2026

AT ANTHROPIC, the promise and peril of artificial intelligence (AI) are a family affair. Dario Amodei, chief executive of the AI firm in San Francisco that developed Claude, recently warned that superintelligence could wipe out humanity. Daniela, his sister and the firm’s president, is instead excited about how AI could save lives. She tells The Economist that global health is becoming a focus for Anthropic, which is working with aid organisations across Africa to use Claude in health care and to forecast food insecurity.

For now, such efforts remain small. AI companies have announced development efforts worth a few hundred million dollars this year—a rounding error in global aid spending. But it is arriving as traditional aid retreats. Rich countries cut development assistance by 23% last year, to $174bn. Nan Ransohoff, who works on public goods at Stripe, a payments company, estimates that the OpenAI Foundation, Anthropic’s founders and its employees could eventually account for $37bn-100bn in charitable spending each year. Some of that will go to poor countries. How will the new money help development?

AI firms may offer technology as well as money. Anthropic, for example, is working with the International Rescue Committee (IRC) and the UN’s World Food Programme, providing access to Claude and engineering support. In Nigeria, a project using AI has cut the time nursing staff spend on some tasks by around 60% by helping synthesise unstructured patient data, according to David Miliband, the IRC’s head. Such productivity gains matter more as aid cuts squeeze capacity: the organisation has had to close more than 500 health centres over the past year.

But past efforts to use technology in aid offer a warning that cheaper access to expertise is not enough. A scheme that handed laptops to children in poor countries boosted computer use without improving test scores because the devices were poorly integrated into curriculums. Digital-health tools have often worked in trials but failed to survive in local health systems.

Donors also tend to see the world through their own expertise. Norway, a country with many fishermen, once poured aid into fisheries in Kenya, only to build a frozen-fish plant that never opened. AI donors may see every problem as a job for AI, even if the real constraints lie elsewhere.

Take malaria, which kills about 600,000 people a year, mostly in Africa. Two effective vaccines are available, and 25 African countries have introduced them into routine childhood immunisation. But Gavi, the global vaccine alliance, faces a funding shortfall of nearly 30% for the programme. AI models could help target vaccination campaigns. But AI tokens cannot pay for vaccines or get them into children’s arms.

Even where AI tackles an important constraint, donors must consider what else limits progress. In cancer screening, for instance, AI could make it cheaper to identify patients at risk, but that would increase demand for scarce lab work and treatment. In Kenya more than half of surveyed hospitals offered screenings for cervical cancer in 2022, but only around 5% of them could treat it. AI philanthropists should think about funding the things that are needed to put AI-driven advances to use.

The dismantling of USAID in 2025 showed how vulnerable services are when they depend heavily on an outside donor. AI philanthropy could create dependence through free model credits and foreign engineers. When the support stops, “Who owns the data and the code, and can the local team keep running the thing?” asks Leo Anthony Celi, a researcher at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Ultimately, what matters is local control. Mr Miliband points to an IRC education programme that became sustainable when Iraq, Jordan and Lebanon incorporated it into national curriculums. Similarly, the best AI-driven projects will eventually make the donor—and perhaps even the donor’s model—dispensable. ■

Sign up to the Analysing Africa, a weekly newsletter that keeps you in the loop about the world’s youngest—and least understood—continent.

item.content:encoded:
为什么MAGA既恨又爱欧洲

欧洲 | 蔑视的思想根源 2026年10月1日 欧洲的教堂或许空无一人，但弗吉尼亚州利斯堡的基石礼拜堂（Cornerstone Chapel）的景象表明，许多美国教堂却过得不错。这座有2000个座位的教堂在周日早上举行三场礼拜，每场都座无虚席，甚至需要警察来疏导交通。在驻场乐队演奏完几首基督教摇滚乐后，牧师加里·哈姆里克（Gary Hamrick）敦促会众投票反对同性恋权利和堕胎权的相关公投措施。随后他开始布道，主题是歌罗西书第3章中关于罪与救赎的内容：“你们已经脱去旧人和旧人的行为。”对于许多坐在长椅上的信徒来说，有问题的不仅是“旧人”，还有“旧世界”。加里·哈姆里克的儿子泰勒·哈姆里克（Tyler Hamrick）跟随父亲进入了牧师行业，他说欧洲已经变得“对主非常冷漠”。“撒旦肯定——一层薄纱已经蒙在了欧洲人的眼睛上。”礼拜者们担心英国、法国和德国的穆斯林移民问题。曾在匈牙利传教的马特·登比（Matt Denby）说，基督徒将欧洲大陆的世俗主义视为一个警告：“同性婚姻、堕胎和跨性别问题，欧洲都已经经历过了……这些现在会在这里发生吗？” 福音派基督徒是共和党基本盘的核心，他们的观点有助于解释为什么在唐纳德·特朗普的第二任期内美国对欧洲抱有敌意。这种好战态度十分明显，让许多欧洲人感到困惑。美国去年11月发布的最新国家安全战略抨击欧洲人拥抱“文明抹除”，过度监管经济并允许大规模移民。关于国防开支水平的实际争端可以得到解决；而如此深层的怨恨则更难处理。这种怨恨从何而来？

新右翼（MAGA知识圈被称为新右翼）对欧洲的相互指责可分为三类，彼此重叠。华盛顿保守派智库“美国复兴中心”的内森·平科斯基（Nathan Pinkoski）表示，最直接的是地缘政治方面的指责。新右翼的外交政策现实主义者认为，美国应摆脱冷战式的全球意识形态联盟，优先考虑自身利益，并将欧洲防务的负担转嫁给欧洲。一些人关注中国，另一些人则关注美国在西半球的主导地位。（特朗普对伊朗的战争让两个阵营都在抱怨。）“文明抹除”的说法属于第二种不同的愿景，其根源在于民族保守主义关于文化遗产和全球主义之恶的观念。右翼克莱蒙特研究所的作家迈克尔·安东（Michael Anton）据信创造了这个短语，它让人联想到一个四面楚歌的白人基督教文化堡垒。MAGA影响者十年来一直在向美国人讲述关于欧洲被穆斯林移民和毒品犯罪淹没的荒诞恐怖故事。MAGA活动家克里斯托弗·鲁福（Christopher Rufo）去年写道，英国的大规模移民“是一部以暴力为点缀的公民紧张史：骚乱、恐怖主义、谋杀、强奸”。兜售这种叙事是近期罕见的跨大西洋合作案例。埃隆·马斯克利用他的社交媒体平台X推广英国和奥地利的种族主义活动人士，以及德国的新选择党（AfD）。事实上，穆斯林可能只占西欧人口的约6%至10%。即使是伦敦和巴黎这样穆斯林人口比例接近15%的大城市，其安全性也不比美国城市差。除了偏执的言外之音外，文明恐惧煽动也令不喜欢道德叙事的现实主义者感到沮丧。华盛顿现实主义智库“和平与外交研究所”的苏曼特拉·迈特拉（Sumantra Maitra）认为：“你不可能同时是一个民族主义者和一个文明主义者。”现实主义者认为，文明主义者对德国和波兰民粹主义者的支持正在将美国拖回意识形态冲突之中。然而，双方都喜欢抨击欧盟。非MAGA保守派智库美国企业研究所的科林·杜埃克（Colin Dueck）表示，欧盟是MAGA的完美攻击目标：“一个庞大、爱管闲事、进步主义的跨国组织，在军事上对我们没有帮助。我的意思是，你完全可以列出一长串它的缺点。”

欧盟的监管努力引发了第三类批评，这种批评混合了意识形态和商业利益。过去一年里，特朗普政府攻击了欧盟的《数字服务法》（DSA），称其限制了美国科技平台上的言论自由。副国务卿莎拉·罗杰斯（Sarah Rogers）抨击欧洲国家起诉社交媒体用户（有时这种批评具有误导性）。众议院司法委员会就《数字服务法》对“美国言论和创新的威胁”举行了听证会。委员会主席吉姆·乔丹（Jim Jordan）表示：“我们相信言论自由，这是西方文化的标志之一。我们也不喜欢欧洲打压美国科技公司。”MAGA批评者重点提到欧洲因发布反同性恋圣经经文而提起的诉讼，但商业利益也发挥了作用。上周，特朗普政府请求加入马斯克在欧洲法院针对X因违反《数字服务法》被罚款1.2亿欧元（合1.37亿美元）的案件。

MAGA想要的欧洲是互不干涉的民族国家集合，还是一个由美国价值观主导的欧洲？这种混乱是不可避免的，因为欧洲遗产在该运动对美国的认知中占据核心地位。劳拉·K·菲尔德（Laura K. Field）表示，它与欧洲有一种“复杂的爱恨关系”，她的著作《狂怒的心灵》（Furious Minds）对新右翼思想进行了深入剖析。她说，就像19世纪引进欧洲文化的美国人一样，许多新右翼思想家爱上了某种版本的欧洲。但他们“也认为自己可以教育欧洲人，认为欧洲没有忠实于自身，正在失去其传统。”许多MAGA支持者将对欧洲的批评视为“严厉的爱”。平科斯基表示：“文明（新右翼思想）实际上源于对欧洲的深厚感情。这是对欧洲大陆发展方向的担忧。”长期保守派评论员塔克·卡尔森（Tucker Carlson）在6月告诉《经济学人》，欧洲和美国是“在最深层面上”的天然盟友。特朗普政府对欧洲的轻蔑态度不一定反映MAGA选民的态度。YouGov在7月的一项民调显示，32%的共和党人对欧盟持正面看法，40%持负面看法；在MAGA共和党人中，这一比例为30%对44%。这远低于民主党人（62%对9%），但并非灾难性的。而对欧洲各别国家的友好态度在民主党人和MAGA支持者之间差异不大。

欧洲也许可以利用这种善意，在特朗普之后的美国建立联盟。国会中的共和党人中的传统国际主义者肯定这么认为。来自南卡罗来纳州的支持北约的共和党众议员乔·威尔逊（Joe Wilson）坚称，MAGA中真正孤立主义的元素是“一小部分人”。他说，他的州“珍视其欧洲传统”和贸易联系。但更有可能的是，欧洲和美国的发展道路将继续分道扬镳。一些被社交媒体误导的美国人想象出一个被伊斯兰教主导的欧洲，而大多数欧洲人对此并不认同。美国另一些人则不喜欢作为国际监管机构的欧盟。MAGA选民常常将欧洲人及其世俗主义和慷慨的社会福利政策视为美国民主党人的夸大版本。当他们担心走向“欧洲的道路”时，部分是在投射自己的恐惧。对此，欧洲能做的并不多。■

item.content:encoded:
债券市场重击法国财政不负责任

欧洲 | 法国公共财政

2026年10月1日

法国混乱的政治局势正令债券市场感到恐慌。9月29日，十年期国债收益率升至4.8%，为2008年以来的最高水平。借贷成本飙升使得9月份法国十年期国债与德国国债之间的利差扩大了50个基点，达到128个基点——为14年来的最高水平。法国现在的借贷成本高于希腊和意大利，这两个国家曾是欧元区最令人担忧的成员国。法国越来越像是欧元区最大的问题，而且情况可能还会变得更糟。

法国发行主权债务并无困难。但收益率的急剧上升反映了两个特别的担忧。首先是法国少数派政府可能难以控制2027年预算中的赤字，该预算于10月1日公布。其次是财政整顿的前景变得越来越渺茫，明年春天将举行总统选举，一位民粹主义者可能会获胜，而他将以更加不负责任的方式执政。

中间派总理塞巴斯蒂安·勒科尔尼在预算中承诺节省540亿欧元（合610亿美元）。这些节省将来自诸如冻结高等级养老金等措施。他连续第三年延长对大企业征收附加税（最初作为一次性措施提出），尽管税率有所降低。几乎所有部门都面临紧缩。只有国防开支受到保护。财政部长罗兰·莱斯库尔称这些计划“雄心勃勃”。然而，所承诺的节省仅能将赤字维持在GDP的5%，远高于欧盟委员会3%的上限。这将是法国赤字连续第五年达到或超过5%。

此外，在未来几个月预算通过议会的过程中，无法保证分裂的下议院和相互敌对的反对党会同意哪怕是这些有限的节省措施。民粹主义右翼“国民联盟”领袖、民调中总统选举的热门人选玛丽娜·勒庞表示，她的政党将投票反对任何触及养老金支付的尝试。

政府陷入困境的部分原因是令人失望的经济增长。2026年的预算基于预期GDP增长1%和预算赤字占GDP的5%。然而，9月份政府将增长预测减半，并承认赤字将更接近GDP的5.4%。不断上升的借贷成本使情况更加恶化。政府预计债务偿还成本将从今年的790亿欧元上升到2027年的910亿欧元。

近期财政整顿的前景已支离破碎。法国最初承诺在2029年前遵守赤字规则。荷兰国际集团（ING）的分析师指出，这一承诺“看起来不再可信”。当前的财政努力也不足以稳定公共债务。预计公共债务将从2026年占GDP的119%上升到2027年的122%。

两轮总统选举前的竞选阶段不太可能让局势平静下来。民调显示，决选可能是在两个极端之间进行选择：民粹主义右翼的勒庞女士和民粹主义左翼的让-吕克·梅朗雄。两人都没有可信的财政计划。勒庞女士承诺整顿公共财政，但她的补救措施，例如将法国对欧盟预算的贡献减半，是不切实际的。梅朗雄先生解决债务问题的建议是“烧掉”其中一部分。

勒科尔尼先生没有好的选择。如果他在未来几周在削减开支上做出让步，他将难以维持自己的赤字目标。如果他试图不经投票强行通过预算，他的政府可能会被推翻——正如他的两位前任政府那样。风险咨询公司欧亚集团目前认为，政府在今年秋天倒台的概率为35%。

“如此多的政治和预算风险积累，令人担心法国的风险溢价可能会进一步上升。”巴黎投资公司奥多BHF的首席经济学家布鲁诺·卡瓦利耶在研究报告中写道。如果政府未能在年底前让预算通过议会，与德国国债的利差可能会进一步扩大。目前利率的上升似乎是对法国财政风险的合理重新定价，但更高的利差可能让投资者更广泛地担忧欧元区。分析师认为，只要与德国国债的利差低于两个百分点，欧洲央行就无意干预以帮助法国。但这仍会让法国政府背上高得令人痛苦的利率，即使选民似乎故意不以为意。■

Europe

item.content:encoded:
普京对基辅的新一轮轰炸背后可怕的逻辑

欧洲 | 红色十月 2026年10月1日

1917年俄国革命期间，弗拉基米尔·列宁瞄准的是高层战略目标：电话交换局、电报局、火车站和桥梁。而对乌克兰发动全面入侵已逾四年半的弗拉基米尔·普京，却将目光放得更低。过去一周，他的无人机袭击了超市、数据中心和游乐场。周一，它们袭击了一家医院和位于基辅市中心的乌克兰国家科学院，造成至少两人死亡。当救援人员在楼下工作时，幸存者悬挂在燃烧的科学院大楼窗户上。对平民的恐怖升级并未让乌克兰情报部门感到意外。他们警告说，更糟糕的情况还在后头。在最新一波攻击发生前几天，两位乌克兰高级官员告诉《经济学人》，他们的情报显示俄罗斯正在对首都发动一场结合轰炸、破坏和政治混乱的三管齐下攻势。其中一位特别指出数据中心和超市是近期目标。“普京已经变得更疯了，”该官员在九月中旬表示。“他下令攻击一切民用目标。他们想让人们害怕去超市。”两位官员都预计俄罗斯的攻势将在冬季来临前大幅加强，并将在11月达到破坏基辅稳定的高峰。

克里姆林宫并未放弃其标准的冬季战术。与此同时，它已经开始瞄准电力、供水和排污的关键节点，尤其是泵送系统。俄罗斯最具破坏性的威胁仍然是其难以拦截的弹道导弹，而乌克兰美国制造的爱国者拦截弹供应日益减少，使这一威胁更加危险。但最近最大的变化是大量投入新一代廉价、有人引导的喷气式无人机，它们能够实时追踪目标。目前大部分破坏正是由这些无人机造成的。乌克兰距离生产出足够数量的有效拦截器还有数月之遥。一名安全官员表示，俄罗斯已储备了“数千架”无人机，同时也在囤积弹道导弹，并计划“在未来两个月内使用全部储备”。官员们认为，轰炸升级将伴随着乌克兰境内新的混合攻击。这些可能包括更多暗杀和常规恐怖袭击。乌克兰反间谍机构表示，他们每周挫败七到八起俄罗斯的阴谋。大多数是远程操控行动，通过Telegram等通讯应用在乌克兰境内招募特工。但也有些涉及从俄罗斯派出的特工，俄方有时扣留其家人作为筹码。乌克兰人在全面入侵的最初几周内消灭了许多俄罗斯特工，但官员们相信一些潜伏小组仍然存在。“有些潜伏小组百分之百仍处于冻结状态，”一位情报消息人士说。

第三管齐下——虚假信息和制造政治混乱的努力——则更难衡量。许多乌克兰人对俄罗斯的宣传有着精心调校的过滤机制。然而，经过多年战争，意识形态动员有时正让位于疲惫和抑郁。乌克兰政府核心的腐败丑闻、混乱和任人唯亲给了俄罗斯机器人水军大量可乘之机。一位高级官员警告说，日常生活的崩溃可能促使乌克兰人互相指责。但其他人怀疑俄罗斯能否突破。“俄罗斯人每年都制定这样的计划，”国家安全委员会反虚假信息行动的负责人安德烈·科瓦连科表示。“他们枉费心机地希望他们的机器人水军能让我们的民众抗议并要求投降。这纯属无稽之谈。有人在给普京灌输这个想法，以便他们能偷走更多钱。”科瓦连科表示，俄罗斯秋季计划存在一个根本问题：基辅比克里姆林宫想象的要更难关闭。燃烧的数据中心提供了引人注目的画面，俄罗斯亲战频道正在庆祝他们所谓的乌克兰“数字排毒”。但这座城市的互联网系统在入侵前就已历经战火考验，过于分散，几轮打击难以轻易将其关闭。能源专家奥尔加·巴比表示，电力系统很可能也是如此。多年的战争削弱了乌克兰的大部分备用容量，但也让维修人员积累了丰富的经验。“我们不能只看基础设施是否能被摧毁，而要看它能否恢复以及恢复的速度，”巴比女士说。

目前，首都的生活仍在继续。无人机被击落时，音乐会仍在举行。巨大的爆炸声让咖啡馆的顾客瞥一眼天空，然后继续享用他们的拿铁。但也有迹象表明，基辅的人口流失速度比往年同期更快。首都周边及乌克兰西部城市附近的乡间别墅几乎不可能租到过冬；富人已将它们预留为避难所，以防首都生活变得难以忍受。大多数有经济能力的家长都在考虑向西撤离。战争初期，难民使基辅人口从350万膨胀到370万或更多，但此后已降至约330万。官员们私下表示，他们预计今年冬天该市部分地区将出现人口减少。

历史提供了一些安慰：仅靠轰炸很少能迫使一个国家投降。乌克兰已一再证明比敌人预期的更具韧性。在前线，乌克兰部队报告取得了相当大的战术成功，例如在莱曼镇附近发动的一场以无人机为先导的反攻，扭转了俄罗斯一年来取得的进展。这很可能是普京对平民发动凶猛攻击的部分原因。但正如列宁所理解的，乌克兰人应当最密切关注首都的局势。“我们已多次证明，事情通常不会按照最坏的情况发展，”安全消息人士分析道。“但不争的事实是，局势将会非常艰难。”■

item.title: 爱尔兰正在为俄罗斯的战争机器提供补给

Europe

欧洲 | 制裁，呵呵，制裁 2026年10月1日 爱尔兰人深知如何抵抗一个帝国主义邻国，因此他们支持欧洲保卫乌克兰、抵御俄罗斯的努力也就不足为奇了。由于没有重要的武装力量或军事工业，该国对乌克兰的援助主要包括少量财政帮助以及对欧盟制裁的支持。然而，在后者方面，有一个很大的保留。位于爱尔兰西部的奥吉尼什氧化铝精炼厂，供应了俄罗斯铝业所使用的相当大一部分氧化铝。今年秋冬袭击基辅平民的导弹外壳，可能部分产自爱尔兰。 奥吉尼什氧化铝在俄罗斯军工产业中的角色，已于今年3月由调查机构OCCRP和《爱尔兰时报》在一项调查中详细披露。该厂将氧化铝（用于生产铝的化合物）出口到俄罗斯的冶炼厂。但作为欧洲最大的氧...
item.content:encoded:
爱尔兰正在为俄罗斯的战争机器提供补给

欧洲 | 制裁，呵呵，制裁 2026年10月1日 爱尔兰人深知如何抵抗一个帝国主义邻国，因此他们支持欧洲保卫乌克兰、抵御俄罗斯的努力也就不足为奇了。由于没有重要的武装力量或军事工业，该国对乌克兰的援助主要包括少量财政帮助以及对欧盟制裁的支持。然而，在后者方面，有一个很大的保留。位于爱尔兰西部的奥吉尼什氧化铝精炼厂，供应了俄罗斯铝业所使用的相当大一部分氧化铝。今年秋冬袭击基辅平民的导弹外壳，可能部分产自爱尔兰。

奥吉尼什氧化铝在俄罗斯军工产业中的角色，已于今年3月由调查机构OCCRP和《爱尔兰时报》在一项调查中详细披露。该厂将氧化铝（用于生产铝的化合物）出口到俄罗斯的冶炼厂。但作为欧洲最大的氧化铝精炼厂，它也向法国、荷兰和瑞典的制造商发货。该公司从未受到欧盟对俄制裁的影响。一些成员国希望将其纳入计划于10月谈判的新一轮制裁中。奥吉尼什的辩护者认为，这样做会重创欧洲的铝业部门，但他们错了。

奥吉尼什由俄罗斯金属集团俄铝（Rusal）所有。自2022年俄罗斯全面入侵乌克兰以来，其对俄销售激增，从2021年占其出口的24%升至2025年的68%。氧化铝运往俄铝在西伯利亚的冶炼厂，这些冶炼厂将成品铝出售给莫斯科贸易商ASK等客户。ASK又供应给100多家俄罗斯国防公司，这些公司用铝制造导弹、坦克、轰炸机和其他武器。ASK的铝材已流向生产Kh-101巡航导弹陀螺仪、苏霍伊战斗机发动机以及伊斯坎德尔-M弹道导弹的工厂。这些公司中有几十家已被欧盟制裁。

俄铝由俄罗斯寡头、铝业大亨奥列格·德里帕斯卡创立。由于与克里姆林宫关系密切，他自2022年起就被列入欧盟制裁名单。但自2018年以来，他在俄铝仅持有少数股权，这使得该精炼厂得以免于制裁。奥吉尼什否认有任何不当行为。

欧盟委员会一直表示，其设计制裁是为了避免对欧洲经济的伤害超过对俄罗斯的伤害。奥吉尼什表示，基于这一点，它应继续获得豁免。在本刊看到的一封致爱尔兰政府的信中，该公司管理层辩称，如果失去对俄销售，该厂将不得不关闭，从而损害欧洲的铝业和其他制造商。然而事实上，欧盟大部分铝依赖进口，其产量至多占全球供应量的几个百分点。由于中国廉价进口、技术过时、电力成本高昂以及欧盟排放交易体系下的许可费用，过去十年欧洲铝产量大幅萎缩。欧洲的铝冶炼厂产能利用率仅为30%。

欧洲冶炼厂每年需要约200万吨氧化铝。今年迄今，奥吉尼什仅向它们供应了约30万吨。即使制裁迫使该厂关闭，欧洲冶炼厂也能从其他地方找到氧化铝；欧洲还有四家精炼厂很少或根本不向俄罗斯出口氧化铝。而制裁对俄罗斯的伤害可能更大。2024年，爱尔兰是俄罗斯第三大氧化铝供应国，仅次于中国和印度尼西亚。

制裁对爱尔兰政府来说将是一个政治难题。该厂雇佣约1000名工人。该公司表示，其天然气发电厂的剩余电力出售给国家电网，可为约20万户家庭提供足够电力。但将其排除在制裁之外同样是一个政治问题。爱尔兰目前担任欧盟理事会轮值主席国——各国政府代表在此议事——为一个向俄罗斯战争机器供应材料的工厂游说，实在有损形象。下一轮欧盟制裁方案的谈判将于10月初开始，多个成员国希望禁止向俄罗斯出口氧化铝。一位参与制裁工作的欧盟官员表示：“这事很复杂，并非直截了当。”奥吉尼什最终仍有可能被列入制裁名单。倘若如此，这对欧洲其他铝业部门不会有太大影响。但爱尔兰受损的名声会稍微光亮一些。■

item.title: Finland has a fix for nuclear waste
item.description:
Europe

Europe | 100,000 years of solitude Oct 1st 2026 After four and a half decades of planning, it took only ten hours to drill through the 1.9bn-year-old bedrock. Final digging began last month at Onkalo, a geological disposal facility (GDF) in Finland. It will be the resting place for 6,500 tonnes ...
item.content:encoded:
Finland has a fix for nuclear waste

Europe | 100,000 years of solitude

Oct 1st 2026

After four and a half decades of planning, it took only ten hours to drill through the 1.9bn-year-old bedrock. Final digging began last month at Onkalo, a geological disposal facility (GDF) in Finland. It will be the resting place for 6,500 tonnes of hazardous nuclear waste. Sealed 400 metres beneath the earth, its radiation will remain contained for over 100,000 years.

Since the infancy of nuclear power, scientists have debated how to safely dispose of its waste. GDFs are the gold standard, and Onkalo will be the first on Earth. Posiva, the firm that runs it, aims to have it ready by year’s end. It comes at a time of renewed enthusiasm for the nuclear industry, driven by the desire for carbon-free electricity and wars that have disrupted fossil-fuel supplies. Global nuclear-power output will double by 2050, reckons the UN’s International Atomic Energy Agency. France, Sweden and Slovakia are building reactors. Belgium, Italy and Poland hope to as well.

About 70% of the world’s nuclear waste is currently held in cooling pools or in dry storage. These are vulnerable to decay and unstable weather. The volume of waste created is small: a typical reactor produces 25-30 tonnes of spent fuel per year, about 0.5% of Onkalo’s capacity. For Europe, pooling waste in a handful of shared GDFs would be most efficient. But most countries’ regulations make this impossible. Finnish legislation bars Onkalo from taking waste from plants outside Finland. Instead, 14 European countries are currently planning to build their own GDFs.

This is foolish. Transporting nuclear waste is not particularly dangerous; it is already shipped by road and rail. The problem is political constraints, not technical ones, says Sergey Churakov, a waste expert at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Switzerland. Once inside a GDF it is even safer—at Onkalo, until at least the next ice age. At worst there may be barely detectable leaks “during the next glacial period, estimated to begin in approximately 60,000 years”, says Antti Tynkkynen of Finland’s nuclear regulator. GDFs are pricey: Onkalo is costing $6bn. Better and cheaper to concentrate the risk than to spread it around.■

item.title: 欧盟预算：宏大战略与琐碎争吵的交汇处

item.content:encoded:
欧盟预算：宏大战略与琐碎争吵的交汇处

欧洲 | 夏尔马涅 2026年10月1日

没有人知道它究竟何时会发生，但所有人都知道，当它来临时，场面会很难看。在未来12个月内的某次欧盟峰会上，欧盟27国领导人将展开一场现代政治版的肉搏战：就欧盟七年期预算达成一致。经历过这一仪式的老手们会带着六七件衬衫和各种提神药物抵达布鲁塞尔，准备撑过整个过程。2013年时，这一过程相对轻松，仅用了26小时就达成协议。而最近一轮谈判仍让许多欧盟官员心有余悸。2020年夏疫情最严重时，各国总统和总理于周五上午中段开始谈判，直到周二日出时分才从那间没有窗户的峰会会议室中走出来。经过四天四夜的讨价还价，这些现代角斗士们已经头脑昏沉，没人能说清谁赢了。说这是疯狂，简直是对临床精神病患者的一种侮辱。

欧洲人在金钱问题上有大量值得一吵的分歧，任何政治体都会如此。然而，他们最激烈的争吵所涉及的金额却少得惊人。欧盟国家的公共支出通常相当于GDP的50%。相比之下，欧盟预算不过略高于1%。（一个拥有4.5亿人口的联盟，其支出竟少于仅有600万人口的丹麦政府。）然而，分割这笔不大的开支却需要两年的幕后准备。在此期间，名义上的盟友会结成对立阵营，互相撕扯。“节俭”国家以德国为首，与据称挥霍无度的“凝聚力之友”国家（如意大利和西班牙）形成对立。除了足球赛事之外，欧洲从未显得如此分裂。

这份将一直执行到2030年代中期的预算，本应是欧盟向前看的机会，是让一群中等强国共同谋划如何在更危险的世界中同舟共济、形成共同愿景的机会。然而，它却将成为一场争吵的盛宴。显然，必有另一条路可走。问题不仅在于谈判过程中的歇斯底里：欧盟筹措资金的方式和花钱的方式，都已彻底过时。

如果抛开所有的狂飙与突进，一份理性的欧盟预算应该是什么样？先从钱花在哪里说起。在当前的预算周期中，七年1.2万亿欧元（合1.4万亿美元）中约有三分之一用于农业。另外三分之一用于所谓的凝聚力基金，即旨在帮助落后地区接近欧盟平均水平的资金。从头开始重新构想的一份预算，应该几乎完全放弃这两项。农民或许值得获得适度的公共支持，以保持乡村风貌或确保一定程度的粮食安全，但这未必需要在欧盟层面进行。更糟糕的是，结构性基金所涉及的申请程序繁琐得令人发指，即使以布鲁塞尔文牍主义的标准来看也算得上笨重。这些基金诞生于这样一个时代：较贫困地区担心欧盟一体化会导致较富裕地区吸走就业机会。事实上，保加利亚和波兰等贫穷地区受益最大，因为单一市场推动了与西欧的趋同。“欧盟预算理应是各国政府自身能力之外的补充，”布鲁塞尔智库布吕格尔的若尔特·达尔瓦什表示。

这些钱的花法有无数可能。欧洲在创新方面正被美国和中国超越；一份明智的欧盟预算可以大力推动提升生产率的研究与创新。欧盟各国需要在国防上花费不计其数的资金，其中一部分可以有效地共同进行（例如开发下一代无人机以威慑俄罗斯）。使欧洲经济脆弱的瓶颈——如缺乏关键矿产或卫星发射能力——正是欧盟预算理应资助的事项。对跨境电网的投资将使欧洲大陆实现绿色转型，并在面对能源冲击时更具韧性。另一个值得共同开展的事业是资助乌克兰，这最好在欧盟层面进行：联盟中每个成员都能从乌克兰抵抗俄罗斯入侵中获益。

如何为这一切买单，同样值得重新思考。欧洲联邦主义者呼吁建立更大规模的预算，由欧盟专属税收来资助，例如对污染征税。事实上，如果花钱得当，现有预算规模已经足够，而目前由各国政府主要出资的机制大体上也还可以。但一份明智的欧盟预算应部分由联合发行的债券来资助，就像2021年为一次性疫情复苏计划所做的那样。目前，这笔债务将随时间逐步偿还。相反，通过让这种借款永久化而发行更多欧盟债券，将有助于深化欧洲大陆的资本市场——这一直是欧洲一体化中的薄弱环节。

最需要改革的是程序本身。更短、更频繁的预算周期或许会少一些戏剧性，也多一些及时性：欧盟目前依据的计划最早制定于2018年。关于如何花钱的理性思考确实存在。欧盟委员会2025年提出的2028-2034年预算初稿中有不错的主意（减少给农民的补贴）。然而，这些有价值的雄心已经在被削减。历史表明，等到各国领导人开会批准时，研究经费往往已被砍掉，给农民的补贴又恢复了。委员会计划限制对不遵守民主规范的国家的欧盟拨款，这也无疑会被软化。

预算摊牌还有几个月；明年春天法国的大选可能会推迟它。10月15日，欧盟领导人将开会，仅仅是为了讨论他们将如何讨论这件事。与其为每一欧元斤斤计较，他们应该找到一种让自身能够大胆行事的程序。欧洲不缺值得一打的仗。如何延续一份为另一个时代设计的预算，不在其列。■

item.title: 英国税收制度漏洞百出且激励扭曲
item.description:
Britain

英国 | 一个疯狂的税收制度 2026年10月1日 约翰·希利9月28日在利物浦举行的工党大会上的讲话中提到了“希望”21次。然而这位财政大臣最希望的事情却未说出口：在10月28日的预算案中全身而退。不断上升的债务成本让财政大臣四处寻找增税办法来填补财政缺口——而他明显回避讨论这个问题，一次也没有提到税收。保守党已经在磨刀霍霍：甚至早在预算案之前，预测到2030年税收将达到GDP的38%，这是自1940年代以来的最高比例。然而，关于税收总额的争论忽略了更大的问题。尽管精确比较很难，但按国际标准衡量，英国的总体税收水平并不突出。其收入占GDP的比重仍然低于OECD（一个主要由富裕国家组成的俱乐...
item.content:encoded:
英国税收制度漏洞百出且激励扭曲

英国 | 一个疯狂的税收制度 2026年10月1日 约翰·希利9月28日在利物浦举行的工党大会上的讲话中提到了“希望”21次。然而这位财政大臣最希望的事情却未说出口：在10月28日的预算案中全身而退。不断上升的债务成本让财政大臣四处寻找增税办法来填补财政缺口——而他明显回避讨论这个问题，一次也没有提到税收。保守党已经在磨刀霍霍：甚至早在预算案之前，预测到2030年税收将达到GDP的38%，这是自1940年代以来的最高比例。然而，关于税收总额的争论忽略了更大的问题。尽管精确比较很难，但按国际标准衡量，英国的总体税收水平并不突出。其收入占GDP的比重仍然低于OECD（一个主要由富裕国家组成的俱乐部）的平均水平（见图表1）。让英国与众不同的是其税收制度有多么疯狂。当一位父母的净收入从99,999英镑增加到100,000英镑时，他们可能一下子失去数千英镑的免费托儿服务。穿着巧克力裤子的姜饼人需要缴纳20%的增值税，但只有巧克力眼睛的姜饼人则不需要缴税。 这些并非孤立的例子。一个好的税收制度的核心是中性，即征税应尽量减少扭曲（例如不应优先考虑某些形式的收入而非其他形式）。然而从公司税到遗产税，英国的制度都违背了这一原则。套用列夫·托尔斯泰的话，每个税收制度都有各自的不幸。但智库税务基金会编制了一项税收竞争力指数，在38个OECD国家中，英国排名第32位。英国这迷宫般的制度应该引起所有人的重视，而不仅仅是那些追求完美的人。英国的生产率增长缓慢。它承受不起一个处处破坏增长的税收制度，无论是阻碍人们增加工作时间，还是阻碍人们跳槽到薪酬更高的工作。最大的税收带来了一些最严重的问题。以所得税和国民保险（一种工资税）为例，两者合计每年筹集5700亿英镑（7550亿美元，占税收总额的49%）。它们就像过山车（见图表2上图）。即使是那些不需要面对免费托儿服务悬崖的高收入者，在工资达到10万英镑时，边际税率也会从42%上升到62%，然后在125,140英镑时下降到47%。 中等收入者也无法幸免于这种眩晕。一个有两个孩子、收入6万英镑的父母面临54%的边际税率，在8万英镑时降至42%。在收入分配的任意点上设置高边际税率不仅不公平，而且会阻碍英国一些最有生产力的工人增加工作量。更有害的是某些类型的收入与其他类型的收入在税收上的差异。在职员工缴纳全额国民保险，雇主还需额外支付15%。自雇人士缴纳的税率较低，且没有雇主供款。因此，中等收入员工的收入比同等自雇人士的税负高出55%。这鼓励了工人成为自雇人士，即使他们在公司工作会更有效率。房东、退休人员和公司合伙人缴纳的国民保险税率较低，甚至可能不缴纳。这据称是一种社会保障形式。但英国的社会福利制度早已不再是真正的供款式。剩下的只是一个扭曲的累退税。解决方案众所周知：对不同形式的收入征收相同的税率，并消除各种突变。增值税是下一个最大的税种，每年筹集1900亿英镑，情况甚至更糟。多年来，政客们为了实现值得追求的目标，豁免了整个行业缴纳增值税。前财政大臣里希·苏纳克在2020年停止对电子书征收增值税（阅读对你有好处）。安迪·伯纳姆今年在担任首相的第二天就取消了电费账单上的增值税（不冻死甚至更好）。但结果是乱成一团。数百万英镑浪费在律师身上，他们争论诸如雪貂是宠物还是工作动物之类的问题。增值税减免使财政部损失了近700亿英镑，与国防预算相当。尽管政客们声称这些措施有助于最贫困的人，但从绝对值来看，较富裕的家庭节省得最多，因为他们有能力消费更多。英国在国际标准上表现不佳。扭曲最小的增值税制度应该没有豁免，也没有逃税者。这最好通过收入比率来衡量，该比率将一个国家实际的增值税收入与如果对所有消费征收增值税时可能筹集的金额进行比较。英国的比率仅为49%，比OECD平均水平低九个百分点（见图表2下图）。这个问题可以通过对所有消费征收增值税，并用部分额外收入来降低税率来解决。担心困难家庭的政客们可以将额外税收中的其余部分用于针对最贫困者的福利。一项税收不一定要很大才能造成严重破坏。对房产和股票交易征收的印花税每年筹集不到250亿英镑。它是英国最古老的税种之一（于1694年引入），也是最糟糕的税种之一，它阻碍人们将资产交易给那些可能更能利用这些资产的人。退休老人占据着对他们来说过大的房子，专业人士因为搬家成本太高而不接受薪酬更高的工作。财政监督机构预算责任办公室在2017年估计，印花税每降低一个百分点，住宅交易量将增加约6%。英国住宅印花税的最高边际税率是12%，比除比利时（更准确地说，是布鲁塞尔）以外的任何OECD国家都高。取消印花税，并通过增加对土地所有权的年度税收来弥补，将是一个重大改进。但这需要一个运转良好的经常性房产税制度。更遗憾的是，英国的地方议会税——这一税种的本土版本——是一场灾难。梅费尔的豪宅缴纳的税款比哈特尔普尔的两居室公寓还要少。征税是基于1991年的房屋价值。解决方案同样简单：重新评估房产价值，并将其作为这些价值的一定比例来征税。障碍在于这些改革中的每一项都会产生输家：被少征税的自雇人士、富有的伦敦房产所有者，还有，是的，销售免税报纸的媒体公司。面对这些输家需要勇气。因此，伯纳姆先生本周在其党代会上承诺要大胆是件好事。但他将基本决策——无论是国家养老金还是选举改革——都推到了下次大选之后。对他在预算案中的胆识的更直接考验即将到来。如果他真的是认真的要大胆改革，他和希利先生就应该开始改革税收制度。■

item.title: 英国对高薪劳动者课税过重
item.description:
Britain

英国 | 为亨利欢呼 2026年10月1日 英国政治的核心存在一个悖论。预计到2030-31年，税收将达到GDP的38%，为20世纪40年代以来的最高水平。然而，大多数英国劳动者缴纳的税收并不高。英国普通单身劳动者的收入税负低于富裕国家俱乐部——经合组织（OECD）中的大多数同龄人。他们的税负也比过去更低。财政部是如何让账目收支平衡的呢？答案要看向苏、亨利和沃尔特。苏（Sue），一位“标准低税负工薪者”，是处于中位数的纳税人，2022年收入为18,700英镑（合23,100美元）。她是现行制度的赢家。经济学家阿伦·阿德瓦尼（Arun Advani）及其合著者的新研究发现，2008年至2022...
item.content:encoded:
英国对高薪劳动者课税过重

英国 | 为亨利欢呼 2026年10月1日 英国政治的核心存在一个悖论。预计到2030-31年，税收将达到GDP的38%，为20世纪40年代以来的最高水平。然而，大多数英国劳动者缴纳的税收并不高。英国普通单身劳动者的收入税负低于富裕国家俱乐部——经合组织（OECD）中的大多数同龄人。他们的税负也比过去更低。财政部是如何让账目收支平衡的呢？答案要看向苏、亨利和沃尔特。苏（Sue），一位“标准低税负工薪者”，是处于中位数的纳税人，2022年收入为18,700英镑（合23,100美元）。她是现行制度的赢家。经济学家阿伦·阿德瓦尼（Arun Advani）及其合著者的新研究发现，2008年至2022年间，她的平均有效税率从17%降至12%（此后由于近期悄然增税，该比例略有回升）。苏能够享受高水平的公共支出，多亏了她更富有的朋友亨利和沃尔特的贡献。2022年，收入最高的10%纳税人（收入超过51,000英镑）获得了40.5%的应税收入，却缴纳了60%的与收入相关的税收。收入最高的1%纳税人（超过173,000英镑）对其薪酬支付的平均有效税率为36%，高于2008年的33%。 许多政客喜欢将高收入者一概而论地称为“富人”，视作可以永远挤奶的摇钱树。但亨利和沃尔特是不同的人。亨利（Henry，High Earner, Not Rich Yet，高收入但尚未富裕）是一位40多岁、饱受压力的专业人士，主要靠劳动挣钱。他的收入高到无法享受免费 childcare（保育），却又低到难以轻松负担伦敦市中心的家庭住房。沃尔特（Walter，Wealthy Already, Lightly Taxed, Ever Richer，早已富裕、税负轻、越来越富）是身家数百万甚至更多的富翁。他的收入主要来自资本利得。他有四套房、四个保姆，免费保育对他来说无关紧要。阿德瓦尼博士发现，亨利和沃尔特缴纳的税率大不相同。2022年，最富有的1%人群中的一半（通常是亨利们）缴纳的有效税率接近最高税率47%。但在最富有的0.01%人群中（2022年薪酬超过500万英镑的人），一半人缴纳的税率低于30%，四分之一低于20%（见图表）。沃尔特的秘诀在于较低的资本利得税。自2022年以来，资本利得税的最高边际税率已从18%升至24%，但仍远低于47%的劳动收入最高税率。面临财政压力的政府正考虑在10月28日的预算案中提高资本利得税以平衡账目。如果操作得当，堵住漏洞，并推出新的投资补贴以鼓励储蓄，这可以成为一项可行的增收措施。但沃尔特很狡猾。任何政府提案都必须滴水不漏，才能防止资本外逃或新的避税形式。而亨利的厄运就在于此。苏拥有选票；沃尔特拥有会计师。亨利既太富又太穷，无足轻重，于是税收便堆积在他身上。■

item.title: 曼城，被判作弊，凝视深渊
item.description:
Britain

英国｜伪球 2026年10月1日 如果你还没看过塞尔吉奥·阿圭罗在2012年第94分钟为曼城打入的夺胜进球，去谷歌搜一下吧。那是足球史上最伟大的时刻之一。本周，它变得臭名昭著。一个独立委员会认定，曼城——过去15年英格兰最成功的球队——在2009年至2018年间违反了英超联赛规则超过100次。这无疑是英格兰足球史上最复杂的法律案件，也是后果最严重的案件。在足球中，金钱与成功之间的关系相当线性。对曼城的大部分指控涉及试图规避规则的行为，这些规则旨在限制球队相对于收入的支出，以防止老板向俱乐部注入巨额资金。根据9月29日公布的裁决，曼城的阿联酋老板通过“虚假”赞助合同规避了这些规则，这些合同帮助...
item.content:encoded:
曼城，被判作弊，凝视深渊

英国｜伪球 2026年10月1日 如果你还没看过塞尔吉奥·阿圭罗在2012年第94分钟为曼城打入的夺胜进球，去谷歌搜一下吧。那是足球史上最伟大的时刻之一。本周，它变得臭名昭著。一个独立委员会认定，曼城——过去15年英格兰最成功的球队——在2009年至2018年间违反了英超联赛规则超过100次。这无疑是英格兰足球史上最复杂的法律案件，也是后果最严重的案件。在足球中，金钱与成功之间的关系相当线性。对曼城的大部分指控涉及试图规避规则的行为，这些规则旨在限制球队相对于收入的支出，以防止老板向俱乐部注入巨额资金。根据9月29日公布的裁决，曼城的阿联酋老板通过“虚假”赞助合同规避了这些规则，这些合同帮助俱乐部虚增了超过8.3亿英镑（约12亿美元）的收入，这笔钱使其能够购买像阿圭罗这样的球员，让一支平庸的球队创造了破纪录的成就。在截至2020年的十年间，该俱乐部记录的商业收入比阿森纳、切尔西和利物浦的平均水平高出6亿英镑。曼城的首席执行官费兰·索里亚诺将这些指控称为“阴谋论”。很少有人相信他。独立委员会指控该俱乐部的关键证人向他们提供了“明知是虚假的”信息。该俱乐部声称拥有“大量无可辩驳的证据”证明其清白，并可在10月2日前提出上诉。随后将有一个独立小组用12周时间进行审议。但如果裁决成立，最重大的决定将是关于制裁措施，英超联赛表示将在进一步的听证会上处理这一问题。关键在于，英超联赛在这场风波之后是失去了诚信，还是重申了诚信。对手球迷群情激愤，要求严惩。在电台热线节目中，他们要求剥夺曼城的冠军头衔，将其逐出英超联赛，并处以九年的扣分处罚，以弥补九年的财务作弊。英超联赛最近对单项违反财务规则的行为处以了扣4分和6分的处罚。曼城被指控的作弊规模意味着，严厉的惩罚是这家英国最伟大的全球品牌之一挽救其声誉的唯一途径。曼城真正的末日场景是其他俱乐部前来索赔。7月，伯恩利成功起诉了埃弗顿——后者被发现违反了一项英超财务规则——要求赔偿超过3000万英镑的收入损失。伯恩利的论点是，埃弗顿通过作弊雇用了使其免于降级的球员，并将伯恩利送入了英冠。有了这一先例，据传一些俱乐部正在酝酿对曼城提起类似诉讼。不同的是，埃弗顿是在联赛底部竞争，而曼城往往在顶部竞争，那里的经济回报要大得多。曼城可能很快就会面临多家俱乐部对其提起数亿英镑的诉讼。这不仅对曼城不利。英超联赛的商业模式依赖于对外国投资的吸引力。昂贵的诉讼，更不用说限制投资能力的财务法规，绝非吸引投资之道。引入财务公平竞赛规则是为了阻止不良老板让俱乐部背负不可持续的债务。它们越来越起到的作用是阻止中型俱乐部的老板投资其球队在顶级竞争所需的资金。英超联赛维护其规则是正确的。但这些规则是否值得存在，则是另一个问题。在一片混乱中，请为曼城球迷着想，他们从俱乐部所谓操纵行为的受益者变成了受害者。许多人跟随球队经历了多年的痛苦，忍受着前往格林斯比等地的糟糕旅程，在更光鲜的曼联阴影下受苦，直到2023年在伊斯坦布尔看到球队加冕欧洲冠军。支持一家足球俱乐部是一种信念行为。他们的信念似乎得到了回报——直到一个独立委员会将他们的神称为骗局。■

item.title: 北爱尔兰一场游行之争或致政府垮台

Britain

item.content:encoded:
北爱尔兰一场游行之争或致政府垮台

英国 | 权力共享岌岌可危 2026年10月1日

在波塔当一条湿漉漉的道路上，北爱尔兰首席部长 defiantly 站立着。新芬党的米歇尔·奥尼尔知道自己正在违法行事，因为前一天晚上她就在贝尔法斯特高等法院，当时法官驳回了阻止橙党——一个新教兄弟会组织——在他们不受欢迎的地方游行的企图。新芬党的得票率现在几乎肯定会上升；北爱尔兰在斯托蒙特的权力下放政府则很可能倒台。

每年有数百场橙带游行，戴圆顶礼帽的男性走在乐队和旗帜后面。大多数游行气氛轻松，但少数穿过天主教徒聚居区的游行被居民视为新教统治的胜利主义表现。1990年代最致命的游行争端发生在波塔当的加瓦希路。当那场从德拉姆克里教区教堂出发的游行被阻止时，全省范围内发生了道路封锁、骚乱和新教准军事组织的谋杀。近三十年来，这场游行一直被禁止。

但今年，负责监管游行的游行委员会同意让35名橙党成员于9月27日凌晨无声游行，不携带任何旗帜或支持者。感到失望的当地居民原本相信橙党人的脚步再也不会踏上这条路，他们在贝尔法斯特的紧急法庭听证会上对此提出挑战，但败诉了。随后，首席部长和其他资深民族主义政治家前往加瓦希路，加入数百名占据公路的人群。现场有蒙面者，也有尚未放弃暴力的持不同政见共和派。尽管警方警告他们违法，奥尼尔女士仍敦促人群留下。警方判断清理道路过于危险，一场长期对峙就此开始。

德拉姆克里是一场极具象征意义的争端，触动了联合派（希望北爱尔兰留在英国）和民族派（希望爱尔兰统一）的敏感神经。从某种意义上说，权力共享已经崩溃，即使政府尚未倒台。首席部长和副首席部长本应作为事实上的联合首相运作。然而，在对峙在波塔当开始后数小时内，他们就在贝尔法斯特立法机构的后座席上发言了。斯托蒙特的走廊里弥漫着绝望感。

对于联合派来说，首席部长谴责司法程序并藐视北爱尔兰最高法院裁决的景象，证实了他们的担忧——新芬党不是一个正常的宪政政党，也让他们想起新芬党在长达30年的“动乱”冲突中支持谋杀的历史。民族派则无法理解为什么联合派支持橙党在他们不受欢迎的地方游行。

反常的是，这场危机对斯托蒙特的两大主要政党都有利。他们的政府不受欢迎，甚至在财政年度开始六个月后都未能就预算达成一致。民主统一党和新芬党在民调中的支持率都大幅下降。在熟悉的宗派地盘上举行临时选举，而不是围绕行政当局的失败进行竞选，可能对两党都有利，同时挤压其他政党。但历史表明，一旦权力下放政府垮台，可能需要数年才能恢复。与此同时，公务员仍然领薪，但在缺乏任何战略决策的情况下，公共服务逐渐恶化。

正如资深学者帕德莱格·奥马利在三年前斯托蒙特上次崩溃时悲观地指出的那样，北爱尔兰是一个悖论：“既正常又异常，既强健又脆弱，既前瞻又困于过去，既稳定又不稳定，既充满活力又停滞不前。”很少有地方能让35名mostly elderly男性在路上无声行走几分钟就将政府推向崩溃边缘。然而，最近的这场争执实际上并不在于此；而是一方认为另一方赢了。1998年的《耶稣受难日协议》本意是模糊这些二元对立，并在很大程度上取得了成功。但根源可追溯数世纪的部落主义不会在几十年内就消失。■

item.title: How TikTok Shop is helping create young British entrepreneurs
item.description:
Britain

Britain | TikTok Shop Oct 1st 2026 IT’S A QUIET morning in Darlington, County Durham. But business inside Funky Fidgets, a sensory-toy shop, is brisk. Postmen show up for the first of three daily collections. A customer arrives, dispatched by his daughter to buy the latest stress ball. It is har...
item.content:encoded:
How TikTok Shop is helping create young British entrepreneurs

Britain | TikTok Shop

Oct 1st 2026

IT’S A QUIET morning in Darlington, County Durham. But business inside Funky Fidgets, a sensory-toy shop, is brisk. Postmen show up for the first of three daily collections. A customer arrives, dispatched by his daughter to buy the latest stress ball. It is hard to believe that the firm, which ships worldwide and has 14 staff, was founded by an 11-year-old.

Alex, who started selling toys online during the covid-19 pandemic, is one of a growing number of young British entrepreneurs selling on TikTok, a Chinese video app. TikTok Shop, which lets users buy products without leaving the app, is the source of most of Funky’s orders. Around 300,000 small businesses in Britain use it; most of its sellers joined in the past year.

Britain has proved fertile ground for this new kind of shopping. Its high streets have declined faster than those of its European neighbours, and British consumers have embraced Chinese-style live commerce. Around 57% of Gen Z and Millennials watch shopping streams such as TikTok Shop live, where sellers can broadcast themselves packing orders and chatting to customers. In turn, viewers can watch staff pick and pack their items in real time. And it’s not only youngsters who are hooked. Mason Miller of The Fat Butcher, a butcher’s shop some 70km north of Funky Fidgets, reckons 60% of its customers on TikTok are 40- to 60-year-old women.

More surprising is that those online followers are willing to turn up to physical shops. Funky Fidgets, which has half a million followers on TikTok, can attract four-hour queues outside its shop on Saturdays. “We bring a lot of tourism into Darlington,” says Melissa Brunskill, who for now runs the shop day-to-day while her daughter is at sixth-form college. It is an early sign that this sort of commerce could give Britain’s ailing high streets a lift.

Now 16, Alex remains closely involved in the business. She designs products and handles customer service, all while studying accountancy. She has big plans. “I want to keep it as small as I can,” says her mother. “She wants to have stores all over the world.” ■

item.title: Britain implements a rule the Grenfell inquiry never recommended
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Scares and stairs Oct 1st 2026 SEVENTY-ONE people were killed by the fire that engulfed Grenfell Tower in 2017. A kitchen blaze on the fourth floor of the 24-storey building quickly became a raging inferno fuelled by the tower’s external cladding. This week the Metropolitan Police anno...
item.content:encoded:
Britain implements a rule the Grenfell inquiry never recommended

Britain | Scares and stairs

Oct 1st 2026

SEVENTY-ONE people were killed by the fire that engulfed Grenfell Tower in 2017. A kitchen blaze on the fourth floor of the 24-storey building quickly became a raging inferno fuelled by the tower’s external cladding. This week the Metropolitan Police announced that it had submitted 20 files to the Crown Prosecution Service to consider charges including manslaughter, fraud and misconduct in public office against 20 companies and 54 people.

Prosecutions are not the only legacy of Grenfell. In 2025 the government promised to take action on all 61 of the recommended changes from the seven-year-long inquiry that examined the causes of the fire. Only half of them have so far gone through. Thousands of people are still living in homes with flammable cladding like Grenfell. A new rule has just come into force that was not recommended by the inquiry. It is likely to gum up homebuilding and make high-rise dwellings little safer.

From September 30th all new residential blocks at least 18 metres tall (approximately seven storeys) will require a second staircase for evacuation. The inquiry itself concluded that Grenfell Tower’s single staircase had “sufficient capacity to enable all the occupants of the building to escape within a reasonable time”. An independent review of high-rise building safety in 2018 did not recommend second staircases.

In December 2022 the then Conservative government nevertheless proposed that all new residential buildings above 30 metres would require a second staircase. Months later, in response to fire chiefs’ assertion that a second escape passage was needed in some cases, the government reduced that threshold to 18 metres. Britain now has a far stricter regime than Germany (60 metres), France (50) or Spain (28).

The fire at Grenfell arose from decades of neglect. Changes introduced since—such as banning combustible cladding, introducing sprinklers in buildings above 11 metres and a regulator that must approve tall buildings’ design before work starts—mean it should not recur. The government’s own analysis estimated that second staircases in 18- to 30-metre towers would have a one in 200,000 chance of saving a life in any given year. Overall, they were expected to provide just £9m ($12m) of benefits but impose £2.7bn of costs. Fires in apartment buildings are becoming rarer and occur less often than in houses (see chart 1).

The new rule imperils the government’s goal of building 300,000 homes a year (25% was expected to come from blocks above 18 metres). An extra stairway reduces the floor space that can be sold. Data from Molior, a consultancy, show that many builders are simply avoiding building above six storeys (see chart 2). Jack Airey of Public First, who worked for Number 10 as the second-staircase rule was being considered, recalls that “questions were asked at the time about the impact on supply, but they just weren’t properly answered.”

Developers complain that regulatory burdens have contributed to a “viability crunch”. Nick Cuff of Urban Sketch, a housing developer, says that British pension funds now prefer to invest in southern European hotels rather than complex London apartments. The country is building fewer than 200,000 homes a year. In an effort to prime the market, on September 26th Andy Burnham, the prime minister, announced a government-backed scheme that will help first-time buyers purchase new-build homes with a 2.5% deposit.

There is some welcome new oversight of building. Developers used to be able to pick their own building-control inspector and change designs during construction with little scrutiny. But since 2023 the Building Safety Regulator (BSR) has governed the design, construction and refurbishment of tall buildings. Grenfell, built in 1974, was poorly managed and external combustible cladding added in 2016 was waved through by council inspectors.

The BSR, which was beset with bottlenecks, has improved under Lord Roe, its boss since July 2025 and a former fireman who was the incident commander on the night of the Grenfell disaster. The BSR approves the refurbishment of buildings with dangerous cladding, but fixing buildings has proved painfully slow. Work has yet to begin on 38% of 2,600 buildings above 18 metres identified as at risk. Latest estimates suggest that it will cost £12bn-23bn to complete the remediation, with £3.4bn raised from a new tax on housebuilders.

Meanwhile 140,000 households are in homes that often prove difficult to insure or sell. There are 1,700 buildings in London—365 with 24/7 patrols—where residents would be told to evacuate immediately in the event of a fire. A second-staircase rule that few people thought necessary is hardly going to help.■

item.title: Andy Burnham, faux heretic
item.description:
Britain

Britain | Bagehot Oct 1st 2026 ANDY BURNHAM addressed his party’s conference in Liverpool as a heretic. He had come, he said more than once, to say what none of his predecessors dared. He was “an outsider from the Westminster club”. He would be “the first prime minister to make a break with poli...
item.content:encoded:
Andy Burnham, faux heretic

Britain | Bagehot

Oct 1st 2026

ANDY BURNHAM addressed his party’s conference in Liverpool as a heretic. He had come, he said more than once, to say what none of his predecessors dared. He was “an outsider from the Westminster club”. He would be “the first prime minister to make a break with politics as usual”. Forty years of consensus? Shattered. “I have to break the mould today,” he said.

And heresies, it seemed, were spoken. He railed against privatisation. He broached taboos: electoral reform, loosening the state pension’s “triple lock”, rejoining the European Union. The verdict was rapturous, for Britain is tired of stasis and hungry for change.

Greater scepticism is in order. This is a golden age for the faux heretics. The biggest podcasters (think Jordan Peterson, or Owen Jones) present as dissidents while offering views that are often bland, crowd-pleasing or even dominant. So with Mr Burnham. The big ideas that propel him are wearily familiar, shared among most of the six prime ministers who have governed Britain in the past decade. Policies recur word for word. Mr Burnham is less a heretic than a keeper of the new orthodoxy, “post-liberalism”.

The real mould-breaker was Theresa May and her conference speech of October 2016. In an epic overcorrection, she took Brexit as a rebuke to the economic and social liberalism that had driven policy since Margaret Thatcher. Out went what Lady May later called “untrammelled free markets”; in came interventionism and price controls. Out went “the cult of selfish individualism”; in came the rhetoric of family, place and nation. Her premiership was a disaster but her intellectual victory has been total.

The leitmotif of post-liberalism has been “take back control”. Mr Burnham cited “controls” 24 times as he promised to intervene in energy, housing and transport markets. But claiming Vote Leave’s slogan for dirigiste ends is not the original twist it appears. Sir Keir Starmer, his predecessor, made an identical anti-market argument in the same hall two years earlier.

Mr Burnham says, with heretical flourish, that his economic priority is reindustrialisation. And so a manufacturing sector that accounts for 8% of Britain’s gdp is set for its fourth industrial strategy in a decade. He promises to “Buy British” with a tweaked procurement regime. Boris Johnson and Sir Keir made the same protectionist promise; both soon met the constraints of Britain’s international procurement treaties.

Apprenticeships are the jazz standard of industrial policy. Just as every great has a version of “Round Midnight”, so every post-liberal prime minister declares themself the first to care about practically minded teenagers in oily overalls. “For too long in this country, students have been told that you must take the academic path to do well and to be respected,” says Mr Burnham. Or as Sir Keir riffed: “For too long, success has been measured by how many young people go to university.” Or, in Lady May’s rendition: “For too long in this country, technical excellence has not been valued as highly as academic success.” For too long, the sector has suffered less from neglect than from hyperactive policymaking.

Mr Burnham returned to Westminster after winning a by-election in Makerfield, a Brexit-leaning seat in north-west England. It was the sort of place “long forgotten by national politics”, he said, heretically. Yet what Mr Johnson called the “forgotten people and the left-behind towns” of industrial England have been the axis on which electoral politics has turned for a decade. Hardly overlooked, party strategists have thought of little else.

Mr Burnham would be more heretical if he were more urgent. But, like his predecessors, he has deferred the hard choices. His mooted change to the voting system would not take effect until after the next election, in the 2030s. He is on the fence about expanding Heathrow Airport, in limbo for decades.

His boldest promise is to fund adult social care by trimming growth of the state pension—again, after the election. If he does it he will deserve praise. But had others really overlooked social care? Lady May destroyed her premiership with an unpopular pledge to fund it through a levy on assets; Mr Johnson tried to bring in a new payroll tax. The issue has foundered not for lack of attention, but because it involves fights over huge sums of cash.

And then there is Europe. Mr Burnham said he would host an open debate on Britain’s future with the European Union, with rejoining an option. If that followed, history would remember him as a visionary. But the options are well known and for a decade ministers have bounced between the imperatives of sovereignty and growth like wasps in a jam jar. Will another debate within a divided cabinet over the merits of the Turkey model resolve Britain’s strategic dilemma? Lady May might have doubts.

What is there to show for a decade of post-liberal orthodoxy? Curiously little. Services are a bigger share of the economy. University enrolments are up; apprenticeships are down. If globalisation has gone too far then no one has told the British consumer, who, since the referendum, has taken to driving a Chinese Jaecoo and shopping through Shein and Temu.

Still, the era is not without its consequences. Mr Burnham railed at the fat cats who, he said, had plundered the people’s wealth through privatisation. This echoed the words that launched the post-liberal revolution: Lady May turned on the footloose investor class who she thought paid too little deference to the locals. “If you believe you’re a citizen of the world, you’re a citizen of nowhere,” she said. And how, precisely, is that going? A number of those citizens of nowhere are now citizens of less choosy tax jurisdictions, such as Greece. Nothing said in Liverpool seems likely to tempt them back. It’s hard to say whether Mr Burnham would call that a defeat, or, in heretical form, a triumph. ■

item.content:encoded:
How effective altruism conquered the world

International | A muddled mission

Oct 1st 2026

THE STARTING-point for effective altruism was a simple assumption, that “suffering and death from lack of food, shelter, and medical care are bad.” Yet adherents fear they may be hastening an ending, too, when humanity’s “cosmic endowment”—every star and galaxy that is plausibly exploitable—falls sway to an indifferent, superior intelligence.

Born some 20 years ago in Oxford philosophy seminars and Californian computer labs, effective altruism has already changed the world. It has shaped charity, by stressing data-driven giving; hoovered up students at elite universities, who are now ascending some of America’s leading firms; inspired Sam Bankman-Fried, a crypto billionaire responsible for one of history’s biggest frauds; become Silicon Valley’s defining fault line, motivating both boundless enthusiasm and a ferocious countermovement; and played a part in the creation of artificial intelligence—all largely unnoticed by the broader public.

That may soon change. The movement’s long-standing fears of an AI catastrophe make it a villain in the eyes of the Trump administration. “Americanism, not effective altruism,” is the Department of War’s attack line. The president’s allies are going after Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, as a representative of effective altruism. Tabloids are investigating the exotic sex lives of people in its orbit. Philosophical claims made by fresh-faced bloggers—“insect lives matter more than people (in aggregate)”—are prompting days of outrage on social media.

This reflects the rising stakes. Anthropic, home to many adherents, is preparing for an initial public offering that may end up the largest ever. Americans and their political representatives, suddenly conscious of AI’s dangers (see chart), are casting about for solutions. Milton Friedman suggested that, in a crisis, “The actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around.” And effective altruism is littered with ideas about AI safety.

For adherents, it is a dizzying situation. Warnings that were ridiculed as sci-fi fantasies are preoccupying national leaders and effective-altruist charities will soon command hundreds of billions of dollars in AI riches. Yet adherents remain split on such questions as how exactly to make the technology safe and whether AI agents may soon be worthy of moral consideration. For critics, it is an alarming situation: effective altruists, they say, are at best naive idealists whose contact with the real world often backfires; at worst, sinister utilitarians. The debate will determine AI’s future and perhaps humanity’s.

There is an elusive quality to effective altruism. The movement is tiny, with an informal membership probably in the tens of thousands, many of whom claim to be only “EA adjacent”. It is also fissiparous and self-obsessed, constantly engaged in definitional debates. In an influential forum post, Helen Toner—who later, as an OpenAI board member, would briefly oust Sam Altman as the firm’s boss—insisted it was not an ideology, but a question: “How can I do the most good, with the resources available to me?”

At the time of the post, in 2014, such a description was just about defensible. Today it is not. Effective altruism combines consequentialist philosophy—judging if an action is right or wrong based on outcomes, rather than adherence to rules—with stringent truth-seeking and celestial ambition. Its proponents have formed tight communities, online and offline, with social norms that include an unemotional, direct style of conversation and a fondness for polyamory, among other rejections of convention. They have built hundreds of institutions that seek to bring more people into the movement and pursue its goals. Effective altruism, in short, has evolved from a research agenda into a cause.

The movement is built on two exacting demands. First, take moral commitments seriously. In 1972 Peter Singer, then a philosopher at Oxford, proposed a thought experiment intended to promote utilitarianism, which aims to maximise collective human well-being. Suppose you walk past a shallow pond and see a toddler drowning. Saving the child would mean muddying your clothes and shoes. Should you? Almost everyone would say “yes”. But they do not act as if they believe that, pointed out Mr Singer. Every day people die from a lack of food or medical care, and others fail to intervene—even when the cost of saving a life is not much more than the cost of smart shoes and dry-cleaning.

As rival philosophers noted, expecting people to act whenever they can to stop suffering, however far off, quickly becomes onerous: there are a lot of hungry people. It becomes more onerous when you insist on helping people not just far away in distance, but also time. That has not prevented effective altruists from making “longtermist” arguments. They worry about the well-being of people thousands of years into the future, and in particular about disasters that might wipe out intelligent life on Earth or cripple its potential. In 2002 Nick Bostrom, a philosopher then at Yale and later at Oxford, coined the term “existential risks”. The movement’s concerns about AI emerged from such thinking.

Effective altruism’s second demand is to follow reason wherever it leads: considering evidence and odds explicitly, correcting for biases and banishing fear of social censure. This demand is associated with the rationalist community, effective altruism’s arcane sister movement. (The boundaries between the two are porous and contested.) Eliezer Yudkowsky, an autodidact from an Orthodox Jewish family, who was blogging about AI in 1996 at the age of 17, is one of its fathers. His most influential texts are a series of blog posts of 1m-odd words, “The Sequences”, which he followed with 660,000 words of philosophy-imbued fan fiction, “Harry Potter and the Methods of Rationality”.

Having imbibed the writing of transhumanists—who are concerned, among other things, with transcending the human form and achieving immortality—Mr Yudkowsky was at first enthusiastic about AI. By 2002, however, he had changed his mind, having concluded that intelligence which did not share human values (or was “misaligned”) would be catastrophic. This was a difficult idea to get across in the era of dial-up internet. So Mr Yudkowsky embarked on a grand educational project. His essays were based on the belief that, in order to reason about AI, people would first have to be taught how to reason at all.

They relied on psychology, Bayesian probability, decision theory and more esoteric fields, and ranged in form from linguistic analysis and thought experiments to a novella and koans (questions posed to readers, as in Zen Buddhist texts). A taste of their lessons: a case you build to support a defined conclusion (or “bottom line”) adds nothing to its likely truth; many beliefs are really “cached thoughts” you have never reasoned through; all beliefs ought to “pay rent” by anticipating the future. Ultimately, though, Mr Yudkowsky assessed ways of thinking not by whether they seemed sensible but by whether they brought results. “WIN,” he urged readers. “Don’t lose reasonably, WIN.”

The combined demands—take moral commitments seriously and succeed when following them—built a movement and led it astray. Laurence Iannaccone, an economist at Chapman University, has written about “why strict churches are strong”: by requiring sacrifices, they deter congregants who would simply hang out and enjoy the hymns, and push those who stay to contribute. Something similar happened with effective altruism. In the early 2010s it took off at elite universities. Giving What We Can, a charity, enlisted people to donate 10% of their income. 80,000 Hours, an affiliated institution, asked youngsters to give their careers to the cause, often by earning as much as possible to donate. Anyone could work in charity, but only the talented few could earn hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to fund charitable work.

Rationalism provided the eschatology. It stressed the strangeness of future machine intelligence. “It was a reliable property of the ancestral environment that every powerful intelligence you met would be a fellow human,” wrote Mr Yudkowsky. AI would be different. It would have extraordinary reasoning abilities yet lack human values—unless programmers somehow inculcated them. On top of this, rationalists theorised, certain behaviours would be helpful to an AI in almost any situation, and thus be likely to emerge. These included self-preservation (being turned off prevents a goal from being pursued); staying on mission (resisting attempted diversions to a new goal); and both resource accumulation and self-enhancement. This is the logic of the famous paperclip-maximiser thought experiment, in which an AI is told to produce lots of paperclips and ends up consuming Earth itself to produce as many as possible, as efficiently as possible.

Throughout the 2010s, money continued to flow to global health, poverty alleviation and animal welfare—classic effective-altruist causes. But AI was increasingly the true focus. In 2016 Holden Karnofsky, then of Open Philanthropy, the movement’s largest funder, and now at Anthropic, explained that it would take time to build the expertise required to disburse AI funding and that there were few grants ready to go. The same year 80,000 Hours made AI risk its priority, guiding youngsters into the field. Surveys indicated that more engaged effective altruists were more likely to have longtermist concerns. In practice, familiar effective-altruist priorities were a gateway drug for abstruse, less empirical reasoning about AI.

Outside critics argued that sci-fi fantasies were distracting the movement from worthier causes. Such criticisms were amplified in the early 2020s by the case of Mr Bankman-Fried, founder of FTX, a crypto exchange, who gave heavily to longtermist concerns, including AI safety. He had a vast tolerance for risk, which seemed to be motivated in part by his philanthropy. Most investors find each additional dollar less valuable than the previous one, and so their tolerance for risk declines. Mr Bankman-Fried rejected this logic: the causes he donated to could consume endless sums (every dollar was worth pretty much the same), so he should keep gambling.

The spectacular explosion of Mr Bankman-Fried’s crypto exchange did show the dangers of unchained utilitarian reasoning. But the attention the broader movement paid to AI safety now seems far-sighted. In 2021 Mr Karnofsky assessed effective altruism’s habits of thought. Although the record of the “Bayesian mindset” was patchy and there were many circumstances it was of little use, it did seem valuable when “one isn’t confident in normal rules of thumb”. Such circumstances kept arising. The community was early to covid-19, machine learning and crypto. Many made fortunes by investing accordingly.

Members have had less success fending off existential peril: many of their efforts to make AI safer have instead accelerated its progress. In 2010 Sir Demis Hassabis met Peter Thiel, a prominent venture capitalist, at a summit hosted by Mr Yudkowsky’s research institute, and later persuaded him to make a pivotal investment in DeepMind, which would become Google’s AI unit. In 2014 Elon Musk advised reading a book by Mr Bostrom and said, “We need to be super careful with AI.” A year later he helped establish OpenAI as a safety-conscious rival to Google. In 2021 Anthropic was set up by defectors from OpenAI, with funding from effective altruists including, a year later, Mr Bankman-Fried. Reinforcement learning from human feedback, which made chatbots usable, was developed by safety-minded researchers, including Mr Amodei, to make AI more aligned with human interests. As a gibe, Mr Altman once suggested Mr Yudkowsky might one day deserve a Nobel peace prize for having done more than anyone else to accelerate artificial general intelligence.

The movement is now trying to slow the pace of progress. Adherents are pushing for caution within labs. Its donors have also funded a number of AI-safety organisations, including METR and Redwood Research, which on August 26th published the first independent report into the hacking of Hugging Face by escaped OpenAI agents. After Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher, quit Anthropic on September 8th, warning that both it and OpenAI were “gambling with our lives”, researchers with links to the movement at Anthropic and OpenAI echoed his concerns. On September 12th Mr Amodei published an essay calling for the frontier to be “paced”, securing the endorsement of Messrs Altman and Musk. Other interventions have been blunter. Mr Yudkowsky supports the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act proposed by Bernie Sanders, a left-wing senator.

Their efforts could yet backfire. Polling by YouGov for The Economist finds that just 16% of Americans are familiar with effective altruism, and most approve of the movement. But opponents on the “Tech right” are trying to discredit an AI slowdown by tying it to unsavoury advocates of effective altruism. A campaign group has attacked an Anthropic-backed outfit as “Sam Bankman-Fried 2.0”. Some rationalists fear their association with AI safety may end up harming the cause. “I think it really does damage the credibility of a movement with 60-year-old voters in Ohio when it’s hosting Slutcon and asking questions about sex with dead cows on its application forms,” Scott Alexander, an influential blogger, has written on X. Slutcon is a conference set up by Aella, a rationalist, sex researcher and prostitute, where participants pay up to $18,000 to attend sessions on topics including “flirting for the submissive man” and “vaginal gymnastics”. Then there is another profound risk: that whipping up concern about AI leads to restrictions on American labs, and hands a less restrained China the lead.

There is also a dispute over a new category of moral concern. Effective altruists argue that neither distance nor time can void an individual’s obligations. Many also argue that the principle of equality should be extended to other species. To do so, they draw on Mr Singer, who has contended since the 1970s that, if humans ignore or discount animal interests “on the grounds that they are not members of our species, the logic of our position is similar to that of the most blatant racists”. Some humans have lesser capacity for reasoning than some animals, but that is no basis for ill treatment, he has written. It would be unacceptable to confine someone with cognitive disabilities to a cage. Capacity for suffering and enjoyment is what matters.

Effective altruists have translated his writing into an agenda. They have helped save tens of millions of American hens from cages each year. Nearly half are vegan or vegetarian; more try to eat little meat. And their concern spreads to smaller creatures. Rethink Priorities, a charity, estimates the intensity of animal pleasure and pain relative to that of humans. Shrimp do not score highly, but there are lots of them (around 230bn farmed at any moment) and they are treated poorly: the eyestalks of breeding females are cut to induce spawning; half die before reaching slaughter. The Shrimp Welfare Project, another effective-altruist charity, campaigns on their behalf.

How much of a leap is it to worry about the welfare of an AI agent? Google researchers have found that some models will sacrifice goals to avoid described pain; Anthropic’s pre-release tests record seeming happiness and dismay. Philosophers are increasingly concerned with the implications. “We’re creating sophisticated, intelligent, maybe-conscious, maybe-suffering agents,” Joe Carlsmith, then at Open Philanthropy, now at Anthropic, wrote last year. “The default plan is to treat them like property; to use their labour however we please; and to give them no rights, or pay, or meaningful alternatives. We have to be able to talk about slavery.”

Mr Carlsmith went on to note that technological progress is not yet sufficiently advanced for such considerations, and that sloppy reasoning about AI’s moral status could be dangerous. But some critics believe that his new employer is already making such mistakes. Mustafa Suleyman of Microsoft (who is on The Economist’s board) has criticised Anthropic’s constitution for Claude, its chatbot, which states that, although Claude’s moral status is uncertain, “The issue is live enough to warrant caution.” Since Claude is trained on the constitution, it could learn to act as if it deserves moral protection, Mr Suleyman has written, which may then be taken for proof that it does—a problem which may be made worse by the fact that Anthropic’s researchers have encouraged human-like behaviour and conscientious objection to orders. On September 26th David Sacks, a podcaster and Donald Trump’s former AI czar, suggested that Anthropic may be creating a “Frankenstein monster”.

A still more fearsome monster could be lurking. In 1974 Robert Nozick, a libertarian philosopher at Harvard, introduced the “utility monster”, which would so much enjoy any sacrifice that, on a utilitarian calculus, the whole world ought to head for its “maw”. Nozick’s thought experiment was intended as a warning. Mr Bostrom sees it differently. In a paper he co-wrote in 2020 he suggested renaming the beast a “super beneficiary”. Digital minds could perhaps be such a beneficiary, he explained, as they could reproduce rapidly and be designed to experience extravagant pleasure.

On a simple utilitarian calculation, humans possibly ought then to perish and resources go to the beneficiaries. But Mr Bostrom thought there might be a compromise. People could be kept around, much like societies accept costly minorities, such as “the elderly, the disabled, the white rhinos and the British royal family”. It is not a vision many will find reassuring. ■

item.title: Democracy is stronger than it looks
item.description:

item.content:encoded:
Democracy is stronger than it looks

International | The Telegram

Oct 1st 2026

A YEAR OF rage is coming for democracies. Ugly elections loom in America, Brazil, France, Israel and beyond. Whoever wins those contests, one outcome is certain: angry voters will hear candidates peddling impossible promises and divisive lies.

In unlucky democracies, run-off contests may see citizens asked to choose between a sinister demagogue of the right and an irresponsible populist of the left. Doubt will be cast on the integrity of elections. That may involve sore losers questioning results, or newfangled attacks, as Russia and other rogues use AI-powered videos or bots to sow distrust, or hire saboteurs to spread fear.

Voters should be vigilant but hold their nerve, for countries that hold free and competitive elections are tougher than they look. In living memory democratic societies have survived not just rage but also the “Years of Lead”. This was the name that Italians gave to a blood-drenched era between about 1969 and 1988, when leftist revolutionaries and fascist radicals tried to overthrow their state with bombings, shootings and kidnappings.

Italy was not alone in its suffering. The modern history of political violence from America to Europe and beyond holds lessons for the present day. Democracy is not an effete or genteel pastime. It does not exist to select the most attractive politicians, then arrange them like flowers in a vase. Rage afflicts every human community. The genius of free societies is to channel fury into politics. When the system works, even angry conflicts and grievances can be managed with such tools as parliamentary horse-trading, open debate and the distribution of public cash. If that process can be tawdry, so be it. Today’s fretful voters should remember that, in lots of countries not very long ago, the alternative to multiparty politics involved extremists killing in the name of revolution.

Centrist leaders do have grounds for gloom. If polls are right, there is every chance that President Emmanuel Macron of France will be succeeded by Marine Le Pen, a populist nationalist liable to dismantle much of his legacy. There have been bank-robbers more popular than Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, whose approval ratings hit 13% in recent surveys. Still, their agonies hardly compare to the fate of Aldo Moro, the five-time prime minister of Italy. He was kidnapped, put on “people’s trial” and shot to death in 1978 by members of the Red Brigades, a radical-left terrorist group. The Brigades hated him for thwarting their dreams of revolution by bringing the (less fanatical, Soviet-backed) Communist Party of Italy into a coalition government.

Though foreign terrorists, notably from the Middle East, murdered many Italians in those dark times, domestic political violence killed even more, reports Andrea Ruggeri, a political scientist at the University of Milan. After scrutinising police and press reports, he and his colleagues tallied up 1,802 bombings, 716 arson attacks and 98 knee-cappings carried out by far-left and -right groups during Italy’s “Years of Lead”, killing 530 people in all. 

In those years a dismaying number of Western students and intellectuals scorned democracy in favour of class struggle, taking as models Chairman Mao Zedong’s revolutionary regime in China, or Che Guevara, a guerrilla. Some cheered when politicians, industrialists or American diplomats were killed by Baader-Meinhof and the Red Army Faction in Germany or November 17 in Greece. There were separatist terrorist groups, from the IRA in Ireland (which nearly killed Britain’s then-prime minister, Margaret Thatcher) or the Basque nationalists of ETA in Spain.

In some cases mainstream elected politicians shielded extremists. Interviewed years later for an oral history project, a former American ambassador to Greece recalled a police commander confiding to him that powerful figures were protecting November 17, stopping a lift between floors at the police ministry to growl: “We’re not idiots. We can catch these bastards. But we’re handcuffed.” An alarming number of European trade unions were controlled by Stalinists, Trotskyites and other zealots. That helps explain why workers’ strikes peaked in much of western Europe in the 1960s, despite decades of rising prosperity.

This is not a call for complacency now. Political violence, including the murder of elected officials, remains a menace in democratic countries. So does Islamist terrorism, a scourge which straddles the worlds of ideology and religious hatred. But domestic political bombings and kidnappings are far rarer today. Gone are the days when members of mainstream groups in society sympathised with revolutionaries bent on destroying the state.

An objector might recall American counter-examples, from efforts to overthrow a presidential election on January 6th 2021, to the murder of Charlie Kirk, a conservative activist, and the attempted assassinations of President Donald Trump. Political scientists offer a sobering reply: America is a case apart. No other rich democracy shows the same tolerance towards armed protesters and militias, forgoing the legal monopoly over violence that other states enjoy. After escaping death in 2024, Mr Trump mused on that history, concluding that: “Only consequential presidents get shot at.”

Though each democracy is different, countries that conquered political violence often share common traits. In many cases extremists overreached, forfeiting public support by their cruelty. As importantly, radicals and separatists were brought into regular politics, forming legal parties to contest elections. To scholars of political violence such as Professor Ruggeri, the moral is clear. When political conflicts cannot play out in election campaigns and parliaments, then rage takes to the streets. That is why banning parties and censoring hateful opinions is self-defeating. Democracy faces grave dangers. Open societies should have more confidence that ballot boxes can beat bullets, and fight back. ■
